Introduction

If you already own REAPER then the world of classical editing including source-destination editing (aka 2-, 3-, and-4-point editing), crossfade editing and more are available to you via the ReaClassical system, which is free and open source. There's no need to spend a great deal of money on Sequoia, Pyramix or SaDiE in order to make editing precise and efficient. As a classical engineer myself, I can say with certainty that what I am about to share with you covers all my recording, editing and mastering needs. Indeed, I couldn't return to the old way of working at this point. Your mileage may vary and I'd love to hear from you if there are functions that you feel might be missing.

  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

What's New in ReaClassical 27

ReaClassical 27 is the biggest release so far. The headline is complete screen reader support, but sighted engineers get a great deal too, including:

  • One-click rendering from the DDP Metadata Editor
  • DDP and PMI import
  • CD Player and Peak and Overs Check
  • Quick Export Recorded Takes
  • A more flexible Smart Import with polywav support
  • Automatic sliver edit removal
  • A new default theme
  • Background recall of mixer snapshots

This page is a short tour. Everything here is covered in detail in the relevant chapter, linked below.

If you are updating from ReaClassical 26, see Update.

New Functions

Working with a screen reader

ReaClassical can now be used from start to finish by a blind or low-vision engineer, with no mouse. Several parts of this are handy for sighted users too.

  • Clara, a REAPER extension for Windows and macOS, lets ReaClassical speak through your screen reader. Install it by typing clara in the Terminal
  • Accessible windows replace the mouse-driven ones (Create Project, Track Setup, Smart Import, Preferences, Notes, DDP Metadata Editor, Mixer Snapshots and more). Sighted collaborators can switch any of them back with Toggle GUI Mode (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+G)
  • Announcements for take number, timeline position, items in a folder, RCMASTER peak and more, with ! to repeat the last one
  • Menu Help (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H) reads out the ReaClassical menu with the shortcut for each item
  • Marker safety: with Clara installed, placing a source or destination IN marker after the existing OUT marker deletes that OUT marker and tells you, instead of leaving a broken pair
  • Keyboard modes let you finish a whole task with single keys: Crossfade Mode (F) to slip, nudge, widen, narrow and shape a crossfade, Item Edit Mode (V) for one item's fades, edges and gain, and Mixer Mode (Alt+S) to mute, solo, pan, flip polarity and set faders without touching track selection. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+E always returns you to the normal keys
  • The Terminal (Ctrl+Enter): type a command such as 1m;2m;3s to mute tracks 1 and 2 and solo track 3. It also installs Clara (clara), sets nudge amounts and converts workflows. The reaper command updates REAPER itself to the version ReaClassical has been tested with (reaper=latest for the newest release, reaper=752 for a specific one). The Terminal works for everyone, with or without Clara. Type help for the full command guide

See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader, Keyboard Modes and The Terminal. Every workflow chapter also has short purple Screen reader users notes.

Note

You do not need a screen reader to benefit from the new keyboard-driven tools below. Without Clara installed, ReaClassical behaves as it always has.

Importing

  • Import DDP (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D) rebuilds the CD track and album metadata layout from an existing DDP image, for checking or remastering
  • Import PMI (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M) does the same from a Pyramix pre-master
  • Polywav import in Smart Import splits a multi-channel file from a portable recorder into mono and stereo tracks using a simple pattern (for example 221: two stereo pairs, then mono). It replaces the old ExplodeMultiChannel function

See Importing.

Recording and monitoring

  • Quick Export Recorded Takes (Ctrl+Shift+D) renders every take so far to WAV, FLAC, Opus or MP3, ready to hand to the producer or musicians on location
  • Toggle Monitor (Ctrl+Shift+A) cycles input monitoring across the input tracks: off, on, tape mode
  • Playback track: a new special track that sends the RCMASTER mix to its own pair of hardware outputs. Toggle it with Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P
  • Disarm All Tracks removes every record arm in one step
  • Take Number Display (Alt+T) shows the current take number in a small window so a colleague can follow along

See Recording.

Rendering

The DDP Metadata Editor (Y) now has a row of Render buttons. Each renders straight away, without REAPER's render dialog, into an Exports subfolder:

  • DDP (Red Book settings) and Cue Audio
  • WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 and MP3 320, one file per CD track, with album and track metadata and cover.jpg/cover.png cover art embedded where the format allows
  • M: Stems, one WAV per mixer track for each CD track
  • Custom, which opens REAPER's render dialog pre-filled with your choices

Sample rate, bit depth and dither are set with dropdowns, and a Tracks box (for example 1-3,5) limits which CD tracks are rendered. Before rendering, ReaClassical also warns about text that DDP and CD-Text cannot hold, duplicated ISRC codes and tracks without a title.

See Rendering.

Mixing

  • Panic Mute (Alt+K) instantly silences everything that can reach your hardware
  • Toggle RCMASTER Hardware Output Mute (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T) mutes or unmutes all of RCMASTER's hardware sends together

See Mixing.

Mastering

  • CD Player (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Y) plays the album back like a physical CD player, including a Transition Review that plays only the joins between tracks
  • Peak and Overs Check (Shift+P) scans the whole project through the faders and routing up to RCMASTER, reports the highest peak and lists every over above a threshold you choose, each with a Go to button

See Mastering.

Editing and navigation

  • Fix Crossfade Sequence Edits (Shift+X) repairs items that have drifted out of alignment across the tracks of a folder, for example after ripple-per-track was accidentally switched off
  • Auto-color project (Shift+K) colors items by take number or folder
  • Auditioning around S-D markers from the keyboard: 6 to 9 (with Ctrl and Alt variants) play short segments around the source and destination markers
  • Folder and track navigation: move to the next or previous folder or track in a folder, jump to the first or last item on a track, move to the start or end of the selected item, and step between crossfade groups
  • Nudging of markers (Ctrl+,, Ctrl+.) and selected items (Alt+,, Alt+.) by a project nudge amount, with larger "x modifier" versions
  • Jump to Time is now split into jumps within the project and within the selected item (J and Ctrl+J)

See Editing and Navigating a Project.

Project management

  • Delete Source Folder (Shift+D) and Delete All Source Items (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Delete) clear out source material in a vertical workflow
  • Support Info To Clipboard (Shift+F1) copies your ReaClassical and REAPER versions, ready to paste into a forum post (without the SWS extension it shows them in a message box to copy by hand)

See Project Management.

New default theme

ReaClassical 27 ships with a redesigned theme as the default: a graphite look with an accent color and redrawn toolbar and transport icons and panels. The Light and two WaveColors (Dark and Light) variants have all been redesigned to match, and the ReaClassical 26 themes are still included if you prefer them.

Improvements and Fixes

Importing

  • Smart Import can now be run on a project that already contains material. New takes are inserted at the edit cursor and only the material that needs to move is moved (26 always added to the end)
  • Import only these takes restricts an import to a session name and/or a list such as 1-3,5,11-15
  • In a vertical workflow, choose the starting folder and a distribution mode: one folder per take, use current folder count, or round-robin across a custom number of folders. A preview shows the result

Editing

  • Every S-D edit, 3-point edit, timestretched insert and delete now removes sliver edits left near the markers, and shortens a crossfade when there is not enough source material for the full length. You are told when either happens

Mixing and automation

  • Mixer Snapshots has a Background auto-recall option, so snapshots keep recalling after you close the window
  • Insert Automation (I) works on a time selection, can stay open for several adjustments in a row, and switches on automation mode automatically (source folders locked, ripple on all tracks). Toggle it yourself with Shift+I or the new A button on the main toolbar, which lights up and animates while the mode is on. In horizontal workflow only ripple changes; nothing is locked
  • New shortcuts to show and hide automation lanes (Alt+D, Alt+E), move between automation items (Shift+←, Shift+→) and envelope lanes (Ctrl+Shift+↑, Ctrl+Shift+↓), and edit an automation item (Ctrl+I)

Project setup and management

  • Mission Control can add the Playback track, move aux and submix tracks left and right in the mixer, and run Auto-color
  • Convert REAPER project now auto-colors the converted project instead of running Prepare Takes
  • Remove Take Names always works on the first folder, so no track needs to be selected first
  • Create Project needs only one track per folder (it was two)
  • Show Statistics (F1) now includes session time with a reset button and your ReaClassical and REAPER versions, and can copy everything to the clipboard
  • Show Statistics also reports the number of items and the length of material outside the album, meaning anything on the first track after a gap of more than 60 seconds
  • Help (H) opens the single-page HTML manual installed with ReaClassical. The PDF manual is gone

A tidier menu

The ReaClassical menu has been reorganized to follow the production from start to finish.

  • Project Setup is now Project Management, and gathers Mission Control, Preferences, conversion, imports and folder tools in one place
  • Auditioning is split into Mouse Hover and Keyboard sections
  • Show Children and Hide Children are combined into a single Hide/Show Child tracks toggle
  • Prepare Takes has been retired. Editing functions find what they need on their own

Shortcuts that changed

If you are used to ReaClassical 26, these existing actions have a new key.

Action 26 27
Record Panel Ctrl+Enter Alt+Enter (Ctrl+Enter now opens the Terminal)
Jump to Time Tab J
Edit Automation Ctrl+Alt+Shift+A Ctrl+I
Add marker and edit Ctrl+M Alt+M
Hide / Show Children E / D E (one toggle)
Prepare Takes T retired

The complete current list is in the Shortcuts Guide.

Under the hood

  • The scripts have been reorganized: the actions you use are in the main ReaClassical folder, while supporting code lives in a lib subfolder and the crossfade editor helpers in crossfade_editor.
  • ReaClassical 27 bundles REAPER 7.78 (26 shipped 7.52)
  • New bundled JSFX: RCModulator (adds gentle movement to a static reverb tail) and the airwindows ports MagicFairyDust2 and Oxide and Seek. RCTimePhase has a fix for high-frequency loss in its interpolation
  • A new Shortcuts Guide and Terminal Command Guide are installed with ReaClassical and open in your browser

Fixes in the 27.0.x releases

  • Smart Import now handles polywav files correctly (27.0.3)
  • Peaks are no longer missing after a polywav import (27.0.5)
  • Auto Solo Folder has moved into the lib subfolder, in line with the other supporting scripts (27.0.5)
  • Polywav import is available in the accessible Smart Import (27.0.4)

For the complete list of changes in every release, see the Changelog.

Documentation

This online manual, located at https://reaclassical.com/manual, serves as the official documentation for ReaClassical. It is also available offline from within ReaClassical as a single HTML page by pressing H (for help). The benefit of the offline version is that it is always in sync with the version of the tools you are using. The structure of the manual is designed to take the user through preliminary remarks, install and update procedures for both ReaClassical and REAPER then a detailed look at workflows from creating a project through to final render. The Reference section follows (a keyboard shortcut guide, recommended free mastering-grade plugins, room tone generation, system tweaks for all three major OSes and frequently asked questions). I highly recommend doing a complete read of the manual and becoming very familiar with the keyboard shortcuts.

Coming from Standard REAPER

It is a very good idea to have a basic fluency in how REAPER works. However, much of ReaClassical relies on different workflows than you will be used to. With that in mind:

Do

  • Learn how items are dragged and trimmed in REAPER
  • Continue using REAPER's mixer to set faders, panning, mute, solo (if you wish)
  • Set up a ReaClassical project by first running Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS)

Don't

  • Engage in any track and folder management (naming & renaming, creating, deleting, reordering etc) outside of Mission Control
  • Set recording inputs outside of Mission Control
  • Create custom track routing outside of Mission Control
  • Create custom item groupings

Avoid

  • Using regular transport controls for recording or playback

Screen reader users (Clara)

The same rules apply, but track and folder management is done with Accessible Track Setup instead of Mission Control. See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader.

Compatibility

ReaClassical runs on any system that is compatible with REAPER. Ready-made builds are provided for ten operating system and architecture combinations: Windows (x64, x86 and ARM64), macOS (Apple silicon, 64-bit Intel and 32-bit Intel) and Linux (x86_64, i686, aarch64 and armv7l, including Raspberry Pi).

ReaClassical, ReaEdit and the ReaClassical plugins are free and open source software, Copyright (C) 2022–2026 chmaha, released under the GNU General Public License version 3 (or, at your option, any later version). Some plugins build on third-party DSP and keep their original licenses, which are stated in each plugin's header. See Licensing for details.

Development Style

Because ReaClassical is released via ReaPack, I have the ability to push bugfixes and new features very quickly into an existing ReaClassical install. Often bugfixes happen within minutes or hours of receiving the report. When I dream up new features, the development often happens in rapid fashion over the course of a few days. However, now that ReaClassical has what I consider a mature feature set, I foresee maintenance and occasional bugfixes becoming more central to the process. This will give me more opportunity to work on this documentation, a complete video tutorial series etc. Part of development is also ensuring that ReaClassical continues to operate as expected with the latest REAPER versions. That's not to say there won't be new features appearing! As the REAPER developers add more new features, I will always check to see what might be useful for ReaClassical.

  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

Versioning Style

ReaClassical uses YY.M.MICRO versioning (where M is a non-padded month) to accurately reflect how current the software is. For example, 27.3.2 would indicate a March 2027 release with 2 further updates which might include new features, improvements to existing functions, or bugfixes. A month of 0 is used when a new year's version is released before January, since 1 would wrongly suggest January: 27.0.62, for example, is the 62nd update of ReaClassical 27 released ahead of January 2027.

  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

Tools and Languages

ReaClassical works on top of REAPER, the digital audio workstation and utilizes ReaPack, SWS Extensions and ReaImGui. ReaClassical functions are coded using Lua. The installers for all operating systems are shell scripts (PowerShell on Windows). All coding is done either in REAPER's ReaScript Development Environment, vscode or kate on Linux. This manual is written in Markdown and built into HTML. The ReaClassical splash screen and banner are created in GIMP.

Licensing

ReaClassical is free and open source software. There is no license key, no activation and no internet check: install it and use it, on as many computers as you like, for your own work including commercial work.

The license

The ReaClassical and ReaEdit scripts are released under the GNU General Public License version 3, or, at your option, any later version. You may use, study, change and share them under those terms. The full text is in the LICENSE file of the project's source repository. The scripts are plain, readable Lua: nothing is encrypted or obfuscated.

Plugins and third-party code

The ReaClassical plugins (RCPlugs) are JSFX files, also released under the GPL. Several build on other people's DSP and keep those authors' licenses and credits, which are stated in each plugin's header and in the Attributions page: for example MIT-licensed code from airwindows, BSD-style code from Thomas Scott Stillwell, and LGPL or GPL code in some of the others.

REAPER

ReaClassical is built on REAPER, which is a separate product made by Cockos Incorporated and is not included. REAPER has a generous evaluation period; after that you buy a REAPER license directly from Cockos. Your use of REAPER is subject to Cockos' license terms.

Your projects are always yours

A ReaClassical project is an ordinary REAPER project: a standard .RPP file with your normal audio files. It opens, plays and renders in any current vanilla REAPER, whether or not you have ReaClassical installed, so there is no lock-in. Your recordings, edits, crossfades, markers and mix all come with it.

Actions that help with problems

Update ReaClassical (Shift+U), ReaClassical Factory Reset (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F) and Support Info To Clipboard (Shift+F1, also in the ReaClassical menu) are always available. Support Info To Clipboard puts your ReaClassical and REAPER versions (REAPER's includes the operating system) on the clipboard and also reads them out in a message box, ready to paste into a support request.

Install

For the complete and recommended experience on Linux, macOS, and Windows, run the single install script provided below.

Warning

You do not need to download or install REAPER separately and you shouldn't try to install ReaClassical inside an existing REAPER setup — ReaClassical comes bundled with its own fully-configured REAPER environment.

Easy Complete Portable Installation (official method)

The installer script is the only official way to install ReaClassical. It sets up a self-contained REAPER together with the required extensions, the ReaClassical resource folder and the right settings in one step. Adding the ReaClassical ReaPack repository to an existing REAPER on its own is not supported. ReaPack is used only afterwards, to keep an installed ReaClassical up to date (see Updating); the installer sets that up for you.

Copy the command for your operating system into either your terminal (MacOS and Linux) or PowerShell (Windows).

MacOS:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://reaclassical.com/macos | sh

Linux:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://reaclassical.com/linux | sh

Windows:

irm "https://reaclassical.com/win" | iex

The installer needs an internet connection. It asks where to install (the default is your Desktop on macOS and Linux; Windows shows a folder chooser) and creates a self-contained folder named ReaClassical_<version> there. It then downloads the REAPER version ReaClassical has been tested with, the ReaClassical resource folder and the correct plugins for your operating system and processor architecture, and sets everything up. Nothing is installed system-wide.

Tip

Note that if the ReaClassical folder already exists, the installer will automatically add a unique suffix to ensure nothing is overwritten.

First Run

Launch REAPER from the new ReaClassical folder. There is no license key, account or activation step: you can start working straight away, for example by creating your first project with Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS).

Screen reader users (Clara)

Install ReaClassical Clara, the accessibility bridge, by typing clara into the Terminal (Ctrl+Enter). See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader.

Update

Updating an Existing ReaClassical Portable Install

Warning

ReaClassical 27 is a new major version. If you are coming from ReaClassical 26 or earlier, do not update in place: run the installer for a fresh copy of ReaClassical 27, which keeps your old install untouched. Updates within the same major version arrive via ReaPack as described below.

Use Extensions > ReaPack > Synchronize packages or press Shift+U (Update ReaClassical). This will sync ReaPack to get the latest ReaClassical functions. If a newer major version of ReaClassical is available, Update ReaClassical tells you so and asks you to install the new version fresh instead of updating via ReaPack.

Screen reader users (Clara)

Update ReaClassical works the same way and reports its result through Clara.

Factory Reset

In the ReaClassical top menu, click on ReaClassical Factory Reset (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F) to return most settings back to those presented at first install. It replaces your keymap, menu, mouse modifiers, render presets, metadata and main REAPER settings (reaper.ini) with the ReaClassical defaults. Existing files are backed up with a .backup extension.

Note

A ReaPack update replaces the ReaClassical scripts but does not touch these REAPER configuration files. If a release changes any of them (for example a new keyboard shortcut, menu entry, toolbar button or render preset), the change will not appear in your install until you run a Factory Reset. A new toolbar button is a good example: its icon arrives with the theme, but the button only shows up once the menu file has been replaced. Check the release notes and run it after updating when a release says so. Any customisations you made to those files are overwritten, so restore them from the .backup files afterwards if needed.

Updating REAPER

It is highly advisable to use the version of REAPER that ships with ReaClassical, which is the version ReaClassical has been tested against. Open the Terminal (Ctrl+Enter) and type reaper to install that tested version. reaper=latest installs the newest public release and reaper=752 (for example) installs a specific one. REAPER closes your open projects (it will ask you to save any unsaved work), installs and restarts. Third-party REAPER update utilities are not included in the install package.

Project Setup

  1. Press Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS)
  2. Select the number of tracks you want per folder
  3. Select a horizontal or vertical workflow

Notes

Track Count

A folder can contain as few as one track. Choosing a single track per folder is intended for a single stereo pair: ReaClassical still builds each folder with two tracks, but the second is kept as a hidden "spare" that can never record, so the folder structure stays consistent everywhere. Folder navigation and Mission Control skip the spare, and adding or deleting tracks later keeps it correctly hidden. Choose two or more tracks per folder for multi-microphone setups.

Workflow Choice

A horizontal workflow approach means that recorded or imported takes are arranged left-to-right in a single folder. A vertical workflow approach is designed for recorded takes of similar material to be stacked vertically.

Warning

You cannot make folders within folders in ReaClassical. Think of it like using a digital or analogue console. There are plenty of ways to control sets of tracks including routing through submixes via Mission Control.

Mission Control

As soon as you press OK, you will see the Mission Control window.

Use this dialog to:

  • Name or rename tracks
  • Set recording inputs manually or automatically based on track naming
  • Temporarily disable recording of a channel
  • Set routing
  • Add "special" tracks: aux, submix, room tone, reference, live bounce, listenback and playback (see Special Tracks below)
  • Change visibility of folders and special tracks in the arrange window
  • Add a track to all folders
  • Delete a track from all folders
  • Re-order tracks in all folders, and move aux and submix tracks up and down
  • Convert between horizontal and vertical workflows
  • Give mixer tracks direct connections to hardware outputs (if mixing using external gear)

Warning

Do not attempt to complete any of the above actions outside of Mission Control!

Additionally you can use Mission Control to optionally:

  • Reach other important ReaClassical windows via a button click
  • Add FX, set volume, panning, mute/solo

Screen reader users (Clara)

Create Project and Mission Control each have a keyboard-driven equivalent: Accessible Create Project and Accessible Track Setup. Both are announced through Clara. In Mission Control the "Toggle GUI Mode" action (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+G) switches between the accessible window and the standard ReaImGui window. See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader.

Special Tracks

Special tracks live alongside the mixer tracks rather than inside your folders. Add them with the Mission Control Add Special Tracks button: enter how many of each you want and press OK. You can add up to 99 each of aux, submix and reference tracks, but only one each of room tone, live bounce, listenback and playback (the dialog shows "(already exists)" once you have one). The live bounce option only appears in a horizontal workflow.

Once added, each special track is listed in the Mission Control Special Tracks section with mute, solo, pan and volume controls, a TCP checkbox to show it in the arrange window, a Routing button, an FX button and a delete button (RCMASTER itself cannot be deleted). Aux, submix and reference tracks can also be renamed there, and aux and submix tracks can be moved left or right in the mixer with the arrow buttons.

Aux and Submix Tracks

Aux (@) and submix (#) tracks are busses that appear in the mixer only, unless you tick their TCP checkbox. Each feeds RCMASTER. ReaClassical treats them in the same way, so the difference is in how you use them:

  • Use an aux for effects shared by many tracks, such as a reverb bus.
  • Use a submix to collect related tracks, such as all the microphones on one orchestral section, so you can balance them together.

To send a mixer track to an aux or submix, click the mixer track's Routing button in Mission Control and tick the destination. Untick RCMASTER there if the track should only reach the master bus via a submix. An aux or submix has its own Routing button too, so you can route one aux or submix into another as well as to RCMASTER.

Room Tone Track

A single room tone track sits before RCMASTER, is shown in the arrange window and feeds RCMASTER. When you add it, ReaClassical imports roomtone.wav from your project's media folder onto it if one exists. Creating CD markers then trims the room tone to the length of the album and adds the fades. See Room Tone Generation and the room tone notes in the mastering section.

Reference Track

A reference track (REF) sits just after RCMASTER, outside the RCMASTER structure, so it is not part of your mix. Import another recording onto it and hover over it with A to audition it and A/B against your own production. By default it is used this way; to use it as an overdub track instead, see Overdub recording and the reference track option in Preferences F5.

Live Bounce Track

In a horizontal workflow, the live bounce track (LIVE) receives a send from RCMASTER and records the rough balanced stereo mix while you record the individual channels. See Live Bounce.

Listenback Track

The listenback track (LISTENBACK) lets you hear a musician who is far away from the recording setup. It is shown in the mixer only, is record-armed with input monitoring on and records nothing. Choose its input channel from the dropdown in the Special Tracks section. Monitoring mutes automatically during playback and recording unless you set the monitoring JSFX to "Always On". See Listenback.

Playback Track

The playback track (PLAYBACK) is a mixer-only monitoring track that receives the RCMASTER mix. It is created muted, and you choose the pair of hardware outputs it plays through from the dropdown in the Special Tracks section. Press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P to unmute it when you want to monitor playback on those outputs. It does not feed the master bus.

Converting a Standard REAPER Project

ReaClassical has the ability to import any REAPER project (available in the top ReaClassical menu via Project Management > Convert REAPER project). Because of the dizzying amount of custom routing and folder hierachy that is possible inside a standard REAPER project, the following occurs during conversion:

  1. A new project tab is created and _converted suffix added to the RPP file
  2. Any folders are flattened
  3. Any empty tracks are deleted
  4. A single folder is formed in preparation for a horizontal workflow
  5. Any effects are moved to the relevant mixer tracks
  6. Any custom routing is removed

At this point, a horizontal workflow is set up and all that is left for the engineer to do is recreate any custom routing using Mission Control. For example, if the original REAPER project used folders to organize orchestral section microphone channels, this would be recreated by clicking on the appropriate routing buttons to disconnect from RCMaster and instead route to one or more newly-created submix tracks.

ReaClassical Preferences

Open via F5 or via Mission Control C. Use the reset button to return every option to its default. Here is a brief description for each one:

S-D Crossfade Length (ms)
The xfade length for all S-D edit functions. Default = 35ms.
CD Track Offset (ms)
The negative offset where CD markers are placed to the left of item starts. This is really for old CD players that could not process quick enough and skipped the start of audio. Default = 200ms.
INDEX0 Length (s) (>= 1)
If you add an exclamation mark to your CD track name in the metadata editor window, a countdown of this set length will visually appear on some CD Players. Default = 3 seconds.
Album Lead-out Time (s)
The amount of silence automatically set at the end of the album. Default = 7 seconds.
No Auto Item Coloring
To remove all automatic coloring of items, set to checked. You can still color items manually via the Colorize function K or add ranking colors via Record Panel or Notes. Default = unchecked.
No Ranking Color
To remove all ranking colors, set to checked. You can still color items manually via the Colorize function K. Default = unchecked.
REF = Overdub Guide
By default, the reference track acts as a way to A/B project material with an external reference audio file. To use as an overdub track see overdub. Default = unchecked.
Add S-D Markers at Mouse Hover
To avoid needing the track to be selected before placing S-D markers, set to checked. This also allows for opening the fade editor F by hover. Default = unchecked.
Alt Audition Playback Rate
The playrate used when using Shift+A etc. Default = x0.75.
Year of Production
Default = The year the project was created.
CUE Audio Format
The audio format that will be rendered to pair with the CUE file. Default = WAV.
Floating Destination Folder
For users who wish to always use the top folder as destination, this visually moves the destination folder just above the placement of source markers, making working in vertical workflow even easier without need for manual vertical scrolling. Note that when checked, the new S-D editing anywhere to anywhere is disabled and destination markers are always associated with the first folder. Default = unchecked.
Find Takes Using Item Names
If the audio material was not recorded in ReaClassical and the filenaming does not include a take number as a suffix, you can find takes based on item names instead by checking the option. Default = unchecked.
Show Only Item Take Numbers
By default, the item names show both session name (if present) and take numbers. For quicker visual location, set to checked to only show padded take numbers. Not available during the album mastering phase. Default = unchecked.
Source Audition Mode
By default, when setting source in and out markers, any previously existing ones are deleted. To convert previous pairs to take marker "regions" for use in the source audition manager Z, set to checked. Default = unchecked.
Marker Offset During Rec/Play (s)
When adding a marker while recording or playing, the marker is placed this many seconds before the current position to allow for reaction time. Set to 0 to disable. Negative values are not allowed. Default = 0.

Screen reader users (Clara)

Accessible Preferences offers the same sixteen options as a keyboard-driven list: Up and Down move between options, Enter edits, Backspace resets the current option to its default and Escape closes. A "Reset All to Defaults" row restores everything. An additional "Other Settings" row holds three accessibility-oriented values: the marker/item nudge amount in milliseconds, the item edge grow/shrink amount in milliseconds (default 500) and the modifier multiplier applied by the "x modifier" versions of the nudge and grow/shrink actions.

Too Long; Didn't Read

I highly encourage the user to read the full workflows documentation for the best chance of becoming an expert in ReaClassical. However, if time is short and you have an upcoming project for which you need to learn just enough to become dangerous, read the following quick workflow summaries.

Create a ReaClassical project

If not done already, create a new ReaClassical project via Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS). The number of tracks should equal the combined number of stereo and mono microphone channels. If in doubt, pick a horizontal workflow.

Quick Setup

  1. Open Mission Control via C
  2. Name your tracks. Use suffixes like "left", "R", "Pair" etc so the automatic record input button can make intelligent decisions
  3. If planning to record, manually or automatically set your record inputs

Important

Save your project before continuing with other workflows.

Recording

  1. Select a parent track of a folder
  2. Press F9. This opens the ReaClassical Record Panel (also available directly via Alt+Enter) and arms the selected folder. Optionally set a session name by clicking the "Session name" text beneath the take number and typing.
  3. Monitor your signal
  4. Use the left-most buttons in the panel (or F9 again) to control recording, pausing and stopping
  5. Add ranking and notes while recording or after the fact
  6. Once all recording is completed, close the record panel (automatically disengages record-armed tracks).
  7. To give the musicians or the producer the takes so far, press Ctrl+Shift+D (Distribute Takes) to export every take as WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320

Importing

While it is always better to record in ReaClassical, occasionally you might need to use audio recorded by other engineers who used a different DAW.

Smart Import

Assuming that the filenaming contains at least a track name and take number separated by underscore e.g. cello_004.wav or cello_T004.wav:

  1. Ensure that you have first created an empty horizontal or vertical workflow ReaClassical project.
  2. Copy or move source material into the media subfolder inside your ReaClassical project folder (or the custom recording path set in Project Settings P, on the Media tab).
  3. Ensure that track names in the project match the channel text in the filenames
  4. If your filenames also contain a session name prior to the track name, the items will be grouped accordingly.
  5. Via the top ReaClassical menu, click on Project Management > Smart Import Audio (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I) and, if using vertical workflow, choose distribution options.
  6. Open Mission Control to add special tracks such as aux & submix, make routing adjustments etc.

Manual Import by Dragging

  1. In your source folder, select items that should be aligned vertically (for example, every channel for particular take) and drag into the ReaClassical project being sure to drop onto one of the folders created by ReaClassical with a track count that matches the number of files you selected. Choose the option "Same time position on separate tracks"
  2. Continue as above for each take
  3. Open Mission Control C to add special tracks such as aux & submix, make routing adjustments etc.

Auditioning

Audition your material via mouse hover + A on parent or child tracks. Use mixer mute and solo buttons to further customize what you hear.

Editing

  1. Set destination IN and OUT markers via 1 and 2
  2. Set source IN and OUT markers via 3 and 4
  3. Press 5 to make the source-destination edit (2-, 3- or 4-point edit depending on how many markers you set), or F4 to make a time-stretched S-D edit (requires all 4 markers), or if only using destination IN marker and both source markers, F3 for an "assembly" or 3-point "insert" edit
  4. To finesse the edit, click on the right item of a crossfade pair and press F

Mixing

  1. Add FX, change routing, and optionally adjust volume, panning etc via Mission Control C
  2. For level changes over a passage (for example, pulling down a spot microphone), select the destination or source track, make a time selection and press I. Set the level and optional ramp in/out lengths and click Apply Automation. A time selection is required
  3. For "scenes" that change the whole mixer from one album piece to the next, open the Mixer Snapshot Manager via Shift+M, select an item on the first (destination) folder, adjust the mixer and click Set Snapshot.... Snapshots are tied to items and are recalled automatically during playback
  4. Before rendering, click Convert to Automation in the Snapshot Manager to turn the snapshots into real automation

Mastering

  1. The album is built on the first (destination) folder, so make sure your finished edit is there
  2. Remove all names from items on the parent track aside from those you want to be track starts. You can clear all items on the folder track via Ctrl+T
  3. Enter track start names via the Notes window N
  4. Press Y to open the metadata editor

Rendering

  1. Press Y to open the DDP Metadata Editor
  2. Choose the sample rate, bit depth and dither (and a track range if you only need some CD tracks)
  3. Click one of the Render buttons at the bottom of the window (DDP, Cue Audio, WAV, FLAC, Opus 160, MP3 320 or M: Stems), or Custom to open REAPER's render dialog first. For a quick loudness and peak check, use the dry run option in REAPER's render dialog (R)

Screen reader users (Clara)

Every workflow above has a keyboard-driven, screen-reader-friendly equivalent. See the Accessibility section for the overview and each workflow chapter for the details.

Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader

ReaClassical is designed so that a blind or low-vision engineer can carry out a complete classical production, from creating a project through recording, editing, mixing, mastering and rendering, using only the keyboard and a screen reader. This section explains how that works. Each workflow chapter also contains short, purple Screen reader users notes wherever the keyboard-driven path differs from the standard one.

How This Section Is Organized

This section is meant to be a complete guide to ReaClassical for blind and low-vision engineers. Read Getting Started with a Screen Reader first, then follow the production through the chapters that mirror the workflow chapters elsewhere in the manual. Keyboard Modes and The Terminal are reference chapters for the modal keyboard controls and the command box.

Clara

Clara is the accessibility bridge that lets ReaClassical speak through your screen reader. It is a REAPER extension available for Windows and macOS. When Clara is installed:

  • ReaClassical announces what it is doing (for example, the take number, the timeline position, the result of an edit) instead of relying on something you must see on screen
  • Windows that are mouse-driven for sighted users, such as Mission Control, Notes, Preferences and the DDP Metadata Editor, open as keyboard-driven accessible windows instead
  • Where a window offers many options, pressing H inside it opens a list of that window's shortcuts that you can step through one at a time with the Up and Down arrows

To install Clara, open the Terminal (Ctrl+Enter) and type clara. See The Terminal. Clara is installed into your ReaClassical folder and REAPER restarts to load it.

Placeholder

Setting up a screen reader on Linux, and the recommended screen reader and settings for Windows and macOS, still need to be documented here.

Accessible Windows and Standard Windows

Every accessible window has a standard (ReaImGui) counterpart for sighted collaborators. Press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+G (Toggle GUI Mode) to switch between them. Any Mission Control, Notes, Preferences, Mixer Snapshots or DDP Metadata Editor window that is open notices the change and reopens in the other mode. This only applies while Clara is installed; without it, the standard windows are always used.

Announcements

ReaClassical provides quick announcements that you can trigger at any time:

Shortcut Announces
T Current take number
Shift+T Highest take number
Ctrl+Shift+J Timeline position
Alt+Shift+J Time within the current item
Alt+F Items in the current folder
Alt+P RCMASTER peak level
! Repeats the last announcement

The Mixer Mode window (Alt+S) lets you move through mixer tracks and hear their input and status.

Keyboard-Driven Windows

Shortcut Window
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R Recording Settings: session name, take number, schedule, overlapping and horizontal takes, clip reporting
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F9 Close Recording Session (stops the Record Panel Daemon)
Ctrl+R Item Rank, with note-taking and item navigation
Shift+N Item Name
V Item Edit Mode
Alt+S Mixer Mode
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+G Toggle between accessible and standard windows

Other accessible windows include Create Project, Track Setup, Smart Import, Distribute Takes, Fix Crossfade Sequence Edits, Automation Navigator, Edit Automation, Mixer Track Grouping, Snapshot Settings, Playback Rate, Peak and Overs Check, Audio Calculator, Show Statistics and Preferences. With Clara installed they replace the standard windows of the same name; see the Keyboard Shortcuts reference for their keys.

Keyboard Modes

For tasks that need many keys, ReaClassical has keyboard modes: Crossfade Mode (F), Item Edit Mode (V), Mixer Mode (Alt+S) and an automatic Recording mode. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+E always returns you to the normal keys. See Keyboard Modes.

Not Using a Screen Reader?

The accessible windows are built for screen reader users, and if you can see the screen you will normally prefer the graphical windows. The keyboard shortcuts, however, are a very fast way for anyone to work. If you want to experiment without Clara installed, the Terminal command debug=on prints announcements to the REAPER console and turns the accessible windows on for the current project.

Getting Started with a Screen Reader

This chapter takes you from nothing installed to a named, ready-to-record project using only the keyboard and a screen reader. Each later chapter in this section follows a stage of the production in the same way, and the workflow chapters elsewhere in the manual link here whenever the screen reader route differs.

1. Install ReaClassical

Run the install command for your operating system from a terminal (macOS and Linux) or PowerShell (Windows), exactly as described in Install. The installer prints its progress as it works, asks where to install and creates a self-contained ReaClassical_<version> folder.

2. Install Clara

Clara is the accessibility bridge that lets ReaClassical speak through your screen reader. It is available for Windows and macOS.

  1. Launch REAPER from the new ReaClassical folder.
  2. Open the Terminal with Ctrl+Enter. A single-line input box asks for a "Command:".
  3. Type clara and press Enter.

Clara is downloaded and installed, any old OSARA plugin in the UserPlugins folder is removed, and REAPER restarts. From then on ReaClassical announces its actions, and its windows open as accessible, keyboard-driven versions. If you want to test announcements without Clara, the Terminal command debug=on prints them to the REAPER console and turns the accessible windows on for the current project; it is stored per project, so a new project starts with it off.

Placeholder

Recommended screen readers and settings for each operating system, and screen reader use on Linux, still need to be documented here.

3. Create a project

Press Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS). The accessible Create Project walkthrough opens and speaks each step:

  1. An input box asks for the number of tracks per folder. The minimum is one, which creates a single stereo track per folder.
  2. Choose a Horizontal or Vertical workflow with ↑ and ↓ and press Enter. A horizontal workflow lays takes out left to right in one folder; a vertical workflow keeps like material together, with the takes of the same piece in separate, aligned folders. Neither is better (see Project Setup); you can convert later in Track Setup.
  3. For a vertical workflow, an input box asks for the number of source folders.

ReaClassical then hands you straight on to Track Setup so you can name your tracks.

4. Track Setup

Track Setup is the accessible counterpart of Mission Control. Open it at any time with C. Use ↑ and ↓ to move through the menu (it wraps round), Enter to choose an item and Escape to go back. Press H for a list of the shortcuts that apply where you are. The main menu is:

  • Track Naming: steps through every mixer track in turn so you can type a name for each. Use suffixes such as "left", "R" or "Pair" so that the automatic input assignment can work out which hardware input belongs to which track
  • Add Track and Remove Track: add a track to every folder (leave the name empty for a default name) or delete one from every folder
  • Reorder Track and Reorder Aux/Submix: pick up a track, move it, and put it down again; the audio and the assigned inputs move with it
  • Special Track Naming, Add Special Track and Remove Special Track: aux, submix, reference, room tone, live bounce, listenback and playback tracks
  • Other Commands: Convert Workflow, Connect All to RCM, Disconnect All from RCM, Auto Assign HW Outputs and Clear All HW Outputs
  • Mixer Control: work on a mixer track's FX chain and routing
  • Set Inputs: assign recording inputs, Auto (from the track names) or Manual

Every change you make here goes through the same code as the equivalent Terminal command, so the result is identical and is confirmed aloud. As in Mission Control, do all track management here and never directly in REAPER. See Mission Control for what each of these does.

5. Set your preferences

Press F5 to open Accessible Preferences. ↑ and ↓ move between options, Enter edits one, Backspace resets it to its default and Escape closes. A Reset All to Defaults row restores everything, and an Other Settings row holds the nudge amount, the item edge grow/shrink amount and the modifier multiplier. See Preferences.

6. Finding your way around

  • H inside a window lists that window's shortcuts for you to step through one at a time.
  • Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H (Menu Help) walks through the whole ReaClassical menu, announcing the shortcut beside each item. Up and Down browse a level, Enter opens a submenu or runs an item and Escape steps back.
  • ! repeats the last announcement.
  • Terminal help opens the full Terminal command guide.
  • Ctrl+Alt+Shift+E (Exit Mode) always returns you to the normal keys from any keyboard mode.
  • Alt+K (Panic Mute) silences everything that can reach your hardware outputs, and unmutes only what it muted.

If a window loses focus, pressing its shortcut again closes it and opens a fresh, focused one.

  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

Recording with a Screen Reader

Everything the Record Panel does for sighted engineers is done for you by the Record Panel Daemon, a background process that keeps the take counter, the session name and the schedule, and speaks the result of each action. You never need to open or use the Record Panel itself.

Before You Record

  1. Make sure every track has a recording input. Open Track Setup (C) and choose Set Inputs: Auto assigns inputs from the track names (suffixes such as "left", "R" or "Pair"), Manual lets you choose each one. If you try to record without any inputs set, you hear "No inputs set -- please assign inputs before recording".
  2. Optionally set the session details in Accessible Recording Settings (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R). It lists the session name, the take number, the scheduled start, end and duration, and switches for allowing takes anywhere, recording takes horizontally and clip reporting, plus a row to start or stop the daemon. Move with ↑ and ↓ and press Enter to change a row. Changing the session name resets the take number to 1, and switching to an existing session name works out the next take number from the takes already recorded.
  3. Select the parent track of the folder you want to record into.

Recording

Everything is driven by F9:

  1. The first press starts the daemon (if it is not running) and arms the folder. You hear "Armed for take 12", or "Folder armed" if there is no session take counter to report.
  2. The second press starts recording: "Recording take 12".
  3. The next press stops it: "Recording Stopped".

There is no need to position the edit cursor first: arming moves the recording position to after the final item in the armed folder.

During a recording:

  • Shift+F9 increases the take number, useful after a false start
  • Alt+F9 starts the next recording section. In a vertical workflow this arms the first source folder, and in both workflows it places the edit cursor 5 seconds after the final item in the project. With "record takes horizontally" on, it arms the next folder down instead
  • Ctrl+F9 pauses
  • Alt+A announces the take number, Shift+T the highest take, and Ctrl+Shift+J the timeline position
  • M adds a marker

A restricted set of keys is active while you record, so that nothing disruptive can be pressed by accident. See Recording mode.

Sending Every Take to Someone on Location

Ctrl+Shift+D (Distribute Takes) exports every take as WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320, to share with musicians or a producer. It has two rows, Render Settings and Export. See Distributing Takes On Location.

Ranking and Notes

After a take, select its item on the parent track and open Item Rank with Ctrl+R. The list is circular: No Rank, Excellent, Very Good, Good, OK, Below Average, Poor, Unusable and False Start. ↑ and ↓ move through it, Enter applies the highlighted rank and Backspace clears it. The window stays open, so you can rank several items in one sitting: ← and → (or Q and W) move to the previous and next item, Space plays and stops, and Escape closes it. The Terminal command ir= sets a rank too.

Item notes, project and track notes, the item name and the take number are in the accessible Notes window (N), and Shift+N opens a quick Item Name window. See Typing Notes.

Special Tracks While Recording

Add a live bounce track (horizontal workflow only) to record a rough stereo mix alongside the individual channels, or a listenback track to hear a musician far from the recording setup, from Track Setup under Add Special Track. Listenback monitoring mutes automatically during playback and recording.

Monitoring and Playback

  • Ctrl+Shift+A (Toggle Monitor) cycles input monitoring on all input tracks that are not disabled for recording, and announces the new state: "Monitor: off", "Monitor: on" or "Monitor: tape mode"
  • Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P (Toggle Playback) mutes or unmutes the playback track ("Playback unmuted" or "Playback muted"). The track is created muted. If there is no playback track you are told so
  • M adds a marker while recording, which you can later use to split a take into subtakes with Shift+S; Alt+M gives a marker a name
  • Alt+T (Take Number Display) opens a small window showing the current take number for a sighted colleague. The daemon opens it automatically

Finishing

When all recording is done, press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F9 (Close Recording Session) to stop the daemon. This disarms the record-armed tracks, the same as closing the Record Panel does for sighted users. The Disarm All Tracks action does the same job for the tracks alone, and you can always switch the daemon off from Accessible Recording Settings.

Checking Your Levels and Disk Space

  • Alt+P announces the RCMASTER peak level. In Mixer Mode, Enter announces the current mixer track's status and I its input
  • The Accessible Audio Calculator works out the disk space needed for a duration of audio, or the time available on a given amount of disk, from units, channel count, sample rate, bit depth and format
  • Track peaks are announced as you move between tracks with ↑ and ↓
  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

Importing with a Screen Reader

Smart Import brings in audio files that are named with a track name and a take number. The screen reader route is a spoken wizard with the same options as the sighted window.

Preparing the Files

Follow the file naming rules in Importing: the take number comes last, preceded by an underscore (cello_012.wav or morning_cello_T012.wav), and the part before it is split at underscores into an optional session name and the track name. Put the files in the project's media folder, or the recording path set in REAPER's Project Settings (P), and make sure you have already created a ReaClassical project.

Running Smart Import

Press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I. ReaClassical announces "Scanning files in project media folder" and then "Scan complete". If the folder also contains multi-channel files, you are first asked to choose between Import Takes and Import Polywav, using ↑ and ↓ and Enter; otherwise it goes straight to the takes wizard.

The takes wizard offers, in turn:

  • Track name order: if the project's tracks have no names yet, this assigns the names found in the filenames to the tracks. The list is in the order the names will be assigned. Pick an entry up, move it up or down and drop it, as in Track Setup's Reorder Track; entries moved past the divider are "not used this run"
  • Distribution (vertical workflow only): One folder per take, Use current folder count, or Round-robin across a custom number of folders (you are asked for the number, with a minimum of 1), and the starting folder
  • Import only these takes (optional): a session name, and a list of takes such as 1-3,5,11-15
  • A final confirmation step before anything changes in the project

Material is inserted at the edit cursor, and files that are already used in the project are ignored. Afterwards, open Track Setup to add aux and submix tracks and adjust the routing.

Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder

Choose Import Polywav to split multi-channel files into mono and stereo tracks. Name the files [sessionname_]Txxx.wav, and enter a channel composition pattern of the digits 1 (mono) and 2 (stereo), for example 221. Enter opens a box to set the pattern (keep or change it there), and ReaClassical tells you how many tracks it gives or why it can't be used. A usable pattern moves on, with the same distribution options as the takes wizard in a vertical project, and a final Enter imports. If the media folder contains only multi-channel files, you go straight to this step. See Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder for how the pattern is applied.

Other Imports

  • Import DDP (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D) and Import PMI (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M) rebuild an album layout from an existing master in a fresh project with an empty destination folder
  • The Terminal command import= runs a Smart Import without the wizard. See The Terminal
  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

Navigating a Project with a Screen Reader

Every move through a ReaClassical project can be made from the keyboard and is announced, so you always know where you are. Mouse navigation also still works as in any REAPER project.

Tracks and Folders

↓ and ↑ select the next and previous track in the current folder and announce its name, its peak level and any mute or solo state. In a project with a single track per folder they move between folders instead. Alt+↓ and Alt+↑ move to the next and previous folder, and D goes to the first folder. Moving to a folder makes it the folder you hear (the others are muted), un-arms any record-armed tracks, selects the item nearest the edit cursor and announces the folder.

If a special track such as an aux, submix or reference is selected, ↓ and ↑ step through the visible special tracks and announce each one with its peak and mute or solo state. At the ends you hear "At bottom of folder", "At bottom of project" or "Last special track".

To go straight to a track, press Shift+J and type part of its name.

Items, Fades and Markers

  • ← and → (or Q and W) move to the previous and next item or fade and announce it as, for example, "Mozart take 3". While editing a crossfade they move through the crossfade, and with an envelope selected they move between its points
  • Alt+← and Alt+→ go to the start and end of the selected item
  • Ctrl+Shift+← and Ctrl+Shift+→ go to the first and last item on the track
  • Shift+Q and Shift+W go to the start and end of the folder
  • Alt+Q and Alt+W go to the previous and next group of crossfaded items
  • , and . go to the previous and next marker

Markers, Regions and Time Selection

These actions are silent in REAPER itself; ReaClassical speaks the result of each one.

  • M adds a marker at the cursor and announces its position. Alt+M inserts or edits a marker, which is how you give it a name
  • Ctrl+M deletes the marker nearest the cursor and says which one. Ctrl+Shift+M moves the nearest marker to the cursor and says which one moved and where. Ctrl+Shift+G deletes all generic markers ("All generic markers deleted")
  • ; creates a region from each selected item, named after the active take ("3 regions created"), and Ctrl+Alt+R deletes all regions ("All regions deleted"). : creates a region from the time selection and L opens the region and marker manager
  • [ and ] set the start and end of the time selection at the cursor and announce its position and, once both edges are set, its length in plain words. Ctrl+] and Ctrl+[ move the cursor to the start and end of the time selection and announce the position ("No time selection" if there is none). / sets the time selection to the selected items
  • 0 deselects all items

Project Tabs

Ctrl+Alt+N opens a new project tab ("New tab") and Ctrl+Tab or NumPad + switches to the next one, announcing the name of the project you land on. See Multi-Project Tab S-D Editing.

Jumping to a Time or a Take

  • J jumps to a time in the project. Type digits that are read from the right, as HH:MM:SS:FF, so 100524 is 10 minutes 5 seconds 24 frames. Start with + or - to move relative to the cursor
  • Ctrl+J does the same within the selected item or a set of crossfaded items
  • Enter searches for a take by number using the file name of the media item. See Finding Takes

Announcements

These speak without moving anything:

Shortcut Announces
T Current take number
Shift+T Highest take number
Alt+F Items in the current folder
Ctrl+Shift+J Timeline position
Alt+Shift+J Time within the current item
Alt+P RCMASTER peak level
! The last announcement again

While recording, the take number is on Alt+A instead of T. In Mixer Mode, I announces the input of the current track and Enter announces its status.

Showing and Hiding Children

Select a parent track and press E to show or hide its child tracks, so that editing a multi-microphone folder is as simple as editing a stereo track.

Project Management with a Screen Reader

This chapter covers the housekeeping around a production: statistics, notes, folders and backups.

Statistics

Press F1 to open the accessible Show Statistics window. It lists the album length, the number of CD markers, the number of items and length of material outside the album (anything on the first track after a gap of more than 60 seconds), the project age, session time, total project length, source material length, number of items, folders, tracks per folder, special tracks and regions, the number of destination S-D edits and item splits, and the FX and automation lane counts. The first entry reads out the ReaClassical and REAPER versions and the name of this computer as your license knows it. Step through the values with ↑ and ↓; you can reset the session timer from the window. See Statistics.

Notes, Names and Ranks

  • N opens the accessible Notes window with fields for the project note, the track note, and for the selected item its name, rank, take number and item note. ← and → (or Q and W) move between items while it is open, and Space plays and stops
  • Shift+N opens the quick Item Name window
  • Ctrl+R opens Item Rank

Folders and Items

  • Ctrl+D (Duplicate folder (No items)) adds a copy of the selected folder's tracks as a new folder, without its items. In a horizontal workflow it first asks whether to convert to a vertical workflow. It announces "Folder duplicated"
  • Shift+D deletes the selected source folder, and Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Delete deletes every item in every source folder. Both are for the vertical workflow and ask you to confirm. "No source items found" is announced if there is nothing to delete
  • Ctrl+Alt+A selects all items in the folder of the selected track. If no track is selected, or the track is not in a ReaClassical folder, you are told
  • Ctrl+V pastes items and announces how many were pasted

Backups, Cleaning and Archiving

Backups, cleaning and archiving are REAPER features that work as described in Project Management. ReaClassical sets auto-save to every 15 minutes. Use REAPER's own File menu for Clean current project directory and Save project as.

Project Tabs

Ctrl+Alt+N opens a new project tab and Ctrl+Tab moves to the next one, announcing its name. Use separate projects or tabs for the discs of a multi-disc album.

  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

Auditioning with a Screen Reader

Auditioning means hearing a folder, or the area around your editing markers, without touching the mouse.

Hearing a Folder

Choose the folder with Alt+↓, Alt+↑ or D (see Navigating a Project). Moving to a folder makes it the audible one, so there is nothing else to switch. Then:

  • Space plays and stops
  • Shift+Space plays and stops, moving the edit cursor along with the playhead
  • Ctrl+Shift+Space returns to the position where you last stopped

In Mixer Mode, S solos the current mixer track and Shift+S unsolos everything.

Hearing the Area Around Your Markers

Once you have set source and destination markers, each of these selects the right folder, makes it audible and plays a short segment, announcing a message if a marker is missing:

Shortcut Plays
6 / 8 3 seconds from the destination IN / OUT marker
7 / 9 3 seconds from the source IN / OUT marker
Ctrl+6 / Ctrl+8 the 3 seconds up to the destination IN / OUT marker
Ctrl+7 / Ctrl+9 the 3 seconds up to the source IN / OUT marker
Alt+6 or Alt+8 from the destination IN to the destination OUT marker
Alt+7 or Alt+9 from the source IN to the source OUT marker

Starting a new audition stops any audition still playing. Use Ctrl+, and Ctrl+. to nudge a marker after hearing it, then audition again.

Auditioning a Crossfade

In crossfade mode (F with Clara installed), Z plays 1.5 seconds either side of the crossfade, X plays the left item up to the center and C plays from the center of the right item. Hold Ctrl or Shift with the key for a longer, 3 second version. See Keyboard Modes.

Note

The mouse-hover audition keys, A and Shift+A (which plays at the custom audition rate), find the folder and position from the mouse pointer, so they are not available from the keyboard. A keyboard version is planned.

  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

Editing with a Screen Reader

Source-destination (S-D) editing is fully keyboard-driven, and every marker and edit action is announced. This chapter follows the editing workflow; the full descriptions of each function are in Editing.

Placing Markers and Making an Edit

Select the folder where you want to place the marker pair (moving to it with Alt+↓, Alt+↑ or D selects it), then:

  1. Place the destination IN and OUT markers with 1 and 2
  2. Place the source IN and OUT markers with 3 and 4
  3. Press 5 for the source-destination edit, F4 for a time-stretched edit (all four markers) or F3 for a 3-point insert edit
  4. Hear the result with the audition keys in Auditioning with a Screen Reader: 6 to 9 play around each marker and Alt+6 / Alt+7 play between a pair

Each marker announces its position, for example "Added source in @ 1 minute 23 seconds". If you place a marker on the wrong side of its partner (a source OUT before the existing source IN, say), the stale partner is deleted and you are told so, which stops an edit silently taking far more material than you intended.

To move the edit cursor to a marker use Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+4. Ctrl+, and Ctrl+. nudge a marker left or right by the nudge amount after you have auditioned it; set the amount with the Terminal command nudge=10 (in milliseconds). Ctrl+Delete deletes all S-D markers.

You can also set both source markers to the edges of the selected items with F12, or the destination markers with Ctrl+F12.

Deleting

Backspace deletes the material between the source IN and OUT markers and ripples later material back with a short crossfade. Ctrl+Backspace deletes it and leaves the silence in place.

Fixing Up the Crossfade

With the right-hand item of the crossfade selected, press F to enter crossfade mode, the keyboard version of REAPER's two-lane editor. It gives you slip, nudge, shift, widen and narrow, fade length and shape, volume, audition and reset and revert, all announced. See Crossfade Mode for the keys. Alt+Q and Alt+W jump between crossfade groups.

If items that should be grouped have become misaligned across the tracks of a folder (for example because ripple-per-track was switched off by accident while dragging items), select any one of them and press Shift+X (Fix Crossfade Sequence Edits). Use ↑ and ↓ to pick which track has the correct edits, Enter to run the fix and Escape to cancel.

Working on a Single Item

Item Edit Mode (V) edits one item's fades, edges and volume from the keyboard. See Item Edit Mode. Shift+R opens the accessible Playback Rate window, which changes an item's rate (rippling the following items) or its pitch. Press H in it for examples.

Nudging

Ctrl+, and Ctrl+. nudge the selected marker left and right (each audition from or to a marker selects it automatically), and Alt+, and Alt+. nudge the selected items. Each nudge is announced, for example "Mozart take 3 nudged 10 milliseconds left". The larger "x modifier" versions are Ctrl+Alt+, and Ctrl+Alt+. for markers and Alt+< and Alt+> for items. Set the nudge amount with the Terminal command nudge=10 (milliseconds) and the multiplier with mod=10, or under Other Settings in Accessible Preferences. In crossfade mode, the crossfade nudge keys are used instead and you are reminded of that.

Other Editing Functions

  • Ctrl+H heals the selected S-D edit, restoring the material it replaced ("Edit healed"). Selecting any one item of a multi-item edit heals the whole edit
  • Ctrl+F finds the source material of an edited item and places a source IN and OUT marker pair there, announcing "Source found" with the take
  • X crossfades two overlapping items when the edit cursor is in the overlap
  • Shift+F removes the fades from items whose edges are not part of a crossfade ("Non-overlapping item fades removed"), Ctrl+V pastes and announces how many items were pasted, and Ctrl+Alt+A selects all items in the folder
  • Ctrl+Alt+C and Ctrl+Alt+M copy or move the destination material into a new source folder, and Ctrl+Alt+P promotes a source folder to the destination
  • Shift+K re-applies the automatic item colors; with a screen reader, colors matter less, but take numbers are still extracted for Enter (find take)
  • Multi-project-tab editing uses Ctrl+Alt+1 to Ctrl+Alt+4 to set project markers in other tabs; see Multi-Project Tab S-D Editing

Note

The Source Audition Manager (Z) is a mouse-driven window and is blocked while the accessible windows are active. A keyboard version has not been written; use the S-D marker keys and the audition keys to compare alternative source takes.

Mixing with a Screen Reader

This chapter follows the mixing workflow. The mixer itself is controlled with Mixer Mode, the snapshot manager and the automation windows are keyboard-driven, and every change is announced.

Setting Up the Mixer

Use Track Setup (C) to add FX chains, routing, aux and submix tracks and hardware outputs. Open a track's FX chain or routing from Track Setup's Mixer Control, or from Mixer Mode with F and R. See Getting Started with a Screen Reader.

Mixer Mode

Press Alt+S for Mixer Mode. ↓ and ↑ move between the mixer, aux, submix and other special tracks, and a single key changes the level, pan, mute, solo or polarity of the current track without touching REAPER's track selection. Grouping keys build groups of tracks. See Mixer Mode for every key. Press Enter to hear the current track's status and I its input.

Mixer Track Grouping

The accessible Mixer Track Grouping window manages groups of mixer tracks. ↑ and ↓ browse the groups and a New group row creates one. Enter opens a group, where you can rename it, choose which special tracks are members and switch on or off whether each of mute, solo, pan, fader, automation and polarity fans out across the group.

Mixer Snapshots

Snapshots are mixer scenes tied to items on the first (destination) folder.

  • To capture one quickly, select an item on the first folder and press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S (Snapshot Add)
  • Shift+M opens the accessible Snapshot Settings, which covers the same ground as the sighted Mixer Snapshot Manager: the bank picker, adding and updating a snapshot, browsing, recalling, deleting and annotating existing snapshots, the recall settings (auto-recall, the gap folder, the nine per-parameter recall switches, switching mid-gap and background auto-recall) and converting to or clearing automation
  • Before you render, convert to real automation. Snapshots recall in real time and are unreliable in a faster-than-realtime render

See Mixing for how recall, banks and conversion work.

Volume and FX Automation

I opens the Automation Navigator, a keyboard walkthrough for inserting automation over a time selection. Make a time selection first. You choose the track (press Shift+Enter to toggle several tracks and apply to them in one pass), then the envelope or FX parameter, then the level and optional ramp in and out. You hear the level you are choosing while you dial it in, but ramps cannot be previewed.

Ctrl+I opens Edit Automation for an existing automation item. Alt+D and Alt+E show and hide automation lanes, Shift+← and Shift+→ move between automation items and Ctrl+Shift+↑ and Ctrl+Shift+↓ move between envelope lanes.

The first time you create an automation item, ReaClassical turns on automation mode, which locks the source-folder items and sets ripple editing to all tracks, so a ripple edit on the destination carries the automation along (in horizontal workflow nothing is locked; only ripple changes). Toggle it with Shift+I; ReaClassical announces "Automation mode on" or "Automation mode off".

Hardware Outputs and Panic Mute

Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T toggles the mute on RCMASTER's own hardware output sends. If any is unmuted it mutes them all, and it only unmutes when all are muted. Alt+K is Panic Mute, which silences everything that can reach your hardware outputs and later unmutes only the tracks it muted itself. It is available in every keyboard mode.

Checking Levels

  • Alt+P announces the RCMASTER peak level
  • Shift+P opens the accessible Peak and Overs Check, which announces the peak position and the number of overs, moves the edit cursor to the peak and lets you browse the overs
  • The Terminal has fast level commands, such as setting a fader or muting by track number. See The Terminal

Mastering and Rendering with a Screen Reader

This chapter takes an edited album through mastering and out to rendered files. The full workflow is described in Mastering and Rendering.

Setting Up the Album

  1. The album is built on the first (destination) folder, so make sure your finished edit is there.
  2. Clear all item names on the parent track except those that start a CD track. Ctrl+T removes all take names from the folder track.
  3. Name the track starts in the accessible Notes window (N) or with the quick Item Name window (Shift+N).
  4. Press Y to open the accessible DDP Metadata Editor.

The DDP Metadata Editor

The editor is a single list. ↑ and ↓ move between the CD tracks, Render Settings, Render, Album and CD Settings. ← and → choose which kind of metadata is read out for the current row: title, performer, songwriter, composer, arranger, message and ISRC (the Album row has its own set of fields).

  • Enter edits the cell you are on in an input box already filled with its value, then stops, so you can press ↓ and Enter repeatedly to fill in one field down every track
  • Ctrl+A applies the current value to every track, Ctrl+R to this and the later tracks, Ctrl+P copies the previous track's value and Ctrl+U copies the album's
  • Invalid ISRC and catalog entries reopen the input box. Read-only cells, such as the automatic album contributors and the automatic ISRC on tracks after the first, tell you why they cannot be edited
  • CD Settings covers Digital Release Only (no CD start offset and no snapping to CD frames), manual ISRC entry, pre and post roll and marker offsets
  • On the Album row you enter the album title, performer, songwriter, composer, arranger, genre, identification, language, catalog (EAN/UPC) and message

Reordering and Offsets

  • To move an album track earlier or later, select its named item in the arrange window and press Ctrl+← or Ctrl+→. It swaps with the track above or below it, gaps are preserved, and any snapshot automation is rebuilt for the new order
  • Ctrl+Y (Reposition Album Tracks) spaces the tracks with a uniform gap in seconds that you enter, leaving crossfaded items intact
  • In CD Settings, the Marker Offsets row adds or clears the CD marker offsets. Shift+O and Alt+O do the same from anywhere. If a cough or a string noise precedes a downbeat, see Marker Offsets

Checking and Warnings

Warnings are announced rather than shown in a dialog. Before rendering, ReaClassical checks for characters that DDP and CD-Text cannot hold (anything outside Latin-1, and embedded line breaks), duplicated ISRC codes and tracks without a title. If a room tone track is shorter than the album, you hear how many seconds short it is.

Rendering

Rendering is part of the same editor:

  1. Move to Render Settings and press Enter. It walks through the sample rate, bit depth and dither in turn (↑ and ↓ to choose, Enter to confirm each)
  2. Move to Render and press Enter. Choose the format: DDP, Cue Audio, WAV, FLAC, Opus 160, MP3 320, M: Stems or Custom
  3. For the per-track formats you are then asked for an optional track range such as 1-3,5. Leave it empty for every track
  4. ReaClassical announces what it is rendering, for example "Rendering FLAC, full album", and renders without opening REAPER's dialog

DDP, Cue Audio and Custom always render the whole album. The files go into the project's Exports folder, as described in Rendering.

Playing the Album Back

Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Y opens the CD Player, which plays the album back like a physical CD player. Its window needs keyboard focus (press the shortcut again for a fresh, focused one). P plays, pauses and resumes, S stops, → and ← change track, ↑ and ↓ fast forward and rewind, D enters a track number, 1 to 9 jump to a track, T cycles the time that is announced (track elapsed or remaining, album elapsed or remaining), R cycles repeat (off, track, album) and Escape powers off. B starts Transition Review, which plays each join (the start of the album, every transition and the end) with a pre-roll and post-roll that you set with W. Press H for the list of keys. See CD Player.

Checking Peaks and Loudness

Shift+P opens the Peak and Overs Check (see Mixing with a Screen Reader). For loudness, REAPER's render dialog can normalize to a loudness target and run a dry run, and the dialog can be opened from the editor's Custom button.

Reports

The metadata editor also writes the album reports (album_report.html and album_report.txt), metadata.txt, and the CUE and CD-Text files, as described in Mastering. The HTML report opens in a browser and is laid out as ordinary headings and tables for a screen reader.
