  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

Keyboard Modes

ReaClassical has several keyboard modes for screen reader users. Each mode swaps in its own set of single-key shortcuts for one kind of task, so a whole task can be done from the keyboard with every action announced through Clara. Only one mode is active at a time, and the keys listed below work only inside that mode.

  • Crossfade Mode, started with F: edit a crossfade
  • Item Edit Mode, toggled with V: edit one item's fades, edges and gain
  • Mixer Mode, toggled with Alt+S: mix without touching track selection
  • Recording mode, entered automatically while recording: a restricted, safe set of keys

In every mode, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+E (Exit Mode) returns you to the normal keys, and it is safe to press if you are not sure which mode you are in. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H (Menu Help) opens a browsable list of the ReaClassical menu with the shortcut for each item, and Alt+K toggles Panic Mute, which silences everything that can reach your hardware outputs (it only unmutes what it muted itself). Space plays and stops, and Q and W move between items, in the same way as outside the modes.

Note

Item Edit Mode and Mixer Mode need Clara. Sighted users work with item fades and the mixer directly, and use REAPER's two-lane crossfade editor in place of Crossfade Mode.

Crossfade Mode

Press F with the right-hand item of a crossfade selected. ReaClassical treats the selected item as the crossfade's right-hand item, and the left-hand item is the one whose end crossfades with it. It selects both of them and their peers across the folder and turns on ripple-per-track until you leave the mode. If the selected item is not the right-hand item of a crossfade, you are told so. Press F again to leave. This gives the same control as REAPER's two-lane crossfade editor, which is used instead when Clara is not installed.

Most keys act on the selected side of the crossfade: select the left item (S), the right item (D) or both (A).

Keys Action
A / S / D Select both / the left / the right item
Z / X / C Audition the crossfade (1.5 s either side of its center) / the left item up to the center / the right item from the center
Ctrl+Z or Shift+Z, Ctrl+X and so on The same auditions with twice the length (3 s)
← / → Slip the item's audio left / right (downstream material ripples)
Ctrl+← / Ctrl+→ Nudge the item left / right
J / K Shift the crossfade left / right (no ripple)
I / U Widen / narrow the crossfade
P / O Grow / shrink the start of the fade
] / [ Grow / shrink the end of the fade
T Cycle the fade shape
N / M Match the right item's fade-in to the left item's fade-out / the reverse
↑ / ↓ Raise / lower the selected item's volume by 1 dB (Ctrl+↑ / Ctrl+↓ for 0.2 dB, Ctrl+0 to reset)
0 Reset both fades to a 35 ms equal-power crossfade
Ctrl+Alt+0 Revert the crossfade to how it was when you first edited it this session

Slips, nudges, shifts, widening, narrowing and fade changes all move by the project nudge amount (set it with the Terminal command nudge=20, in milliseconds). Most actions also have a larger "x modifier" version on the same key with Shift or Ctrl added (for example Shift+← or Ctrl+J), which moves by the nudge amount multiplied by the modifier amount (Terminal command mod=10). Some actions are blocked when both items are selected, because they only make sense for one side.

Each keyboard crossfade action announces what it did, and the Announce Selected Items action tells you whether the left item, the right item or both are selected. Outside crossfade mode, Alt+Q and Alt+W jump between crossfade groups.

Item Edit Mode

Toggle with V. The mode works on the item that is currently selected, and follows the selection: move to another item with any navigation key (Left, Right, Q, W or a click) and the mode announces the new item and which side of the fade is active. Press V again to leave.

Keys Action
S / D Choose the fade in / the fade out as the active side
I / U Grow / shrink that fade
T Cycle the fade shape
0 Reset the fade
P / O Grow / shrink the left edge of the item
] / [ Grow / shrink the right edge of the item
↑ / ↓ Raise / lower the item's volume by 1 dB (Ctrl+↑ / Ctrl+↓ for 0.2 dB, Ctrl+0 to reset)
Ctrl+S Save the project

Holding Shift with a growing or shrinking key (for example Shift+I or Shift+P) uses the larger "x modifier" amount. Edges move by the Item Edge Grow/Shrink Amount (default 500 ms), and the modifier multiplier applies on top. Set both in Accessible Preferences under Other Settings.

Mixer Mode

Toggle with Alt+S. Mixer Mode acts on a current target, a mixer, aux, submix or other special track that you move between with ↓ and ↑. It never changes REAPER's real track selection, so folder, item and take navigation carries on as normal while you mix. Press Alt+S again to leave.

Keys Action
↓ / ↑ Next / previous special track
M, S, P Toggle mute, solo, polarity on the target
Shift+M, Shift+S, Shift+P Unmute all, unsolo all, normal polarity on all
= / - Raise / lower the fader (+ / _ for larger steps)
0 or U Fader to unity (Shift+U for all tracks)
K Fader to minus infinity (Shift+K for all tracks)
← / → Pan left / right (Shift+← / Shift+→ for larger steps)
C Center the pan (Shift+C for all tracks)
F Open the target's FX chain
R Open the target's routing
I Announce the target's input
Enter Announce the target's status
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S Set a mixer snapshot
Shift+J Jump to a track by typing part of its name

Grouping keys: G groups tracks (use Alt+G to group a multi-selection), Alt+L lists the groups, L reports the current group, T toggles grouping for the current group and Ctrl+T toggles it for all groups. Ctrl+G removes the current group and Ctrl+Shift+G removes all groups.

Navigation also works inside Mixer Mode: Alt+↓ and Alt+↑ move between folders, Shift+D goes to the first folder, and Q and W move between items.

Recording Mode

While a recording is in progress, ReaClassical automatically switches to a restricted set of keys, so nothing disruptive can be pressed by accident. The keys available are:

Keys Action
F9 Stop recording
Shift+F9 Increment the take number
Ctrl+F9 Pause
Alt+A / Shift+T Announce the take number / the highest take
Ctrl+Shift+J Announce the timeline position
M Add a marker
S Split items at the cursor
E Show or hide children
Ctrl+Alt+→ and similar Zoom to the whole project
Alt+S Mixer Mode (leaving it returns you to Recording mode)
Ctrl+Enter The Terminal

Zoom and view keys are available too. Stopping the recording returns you to the normal keys.

  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

The Terminal

The Terminal is a single text-entry dialog opened with Ctrl+Enter. Type a command, press Enter, and ReaClassical carries it out and speaks a confirmation. It is built for screen reader use and covers fast power-mixer moves (mute, solo, pan, fader, peak, polarity), workflow conversion, importing audio, nudge and modifier amounts, and setup utilities.

You can run several commands at once by separating them with a semicolon: 1m;2m;3s mutes tracks 1 and 2 and solos track 3.

Setup Commands

Command What it does
clara Download and install Clara (Windows and macOS), then restart REAPER
reaper Install the REAPER version ReaClassical has been tested with. reaper=latest installs the newest public version and reaper=752 (for example) a specific one
debug=on / debug=off Also print announcements to the REAPER console. Stored per project
help Open the full Terminal command guide in your browser

Full Command Guide

The complete list of commands, with the target syntax used to select tracks, aux and submix tracks, the RCMASTER and reference tracks, is in the Terminal Command Guide. It is also installed with ReaClassical and opens when you type help.

Recording

Now that you have decided on a workflow, we can start recording!

Manually Setting Inputs

Use Mission Control C to set recording inputs and panning manually or automatically based on track name. For automatic assignment, add text like "Left", "R", "Pair", "2ch" etc. as a suffix and press Auto Rec Inputs.

Primary and Secondary Recording Paths

By default, ReaClassical creates a media subfolder within the project directory to serve as the primary location for storing audio files. If a secondary recording folder is specified, all tracks are automatically configured to use it. To set the secondary recording path or change the primary path, open Project Settings by pressing P, then select the "Media" tab.

Easy Steps to Record

  1. Select a parent track of a folder
  2. Press F9. This opens the ReaClassical Record Panel (also available directly via Alt+Enter) and arms the selected folder. Optionally set a session name by clicking the "Session name" text beneath the take number and typing.
  3. Monitor your signal
  4. Use the left-most buttons in the panel (or F9 again) to control recording, pausing and stopping
  5. Add ranking and notes while recording or after the fact
  6. Once all recording is completed, close the record panel (automatically disengages record-armed tracks).

Screen reader users (Clara)

No panel is needed: pressing F9 starts the Record Panel Daemon, which runs in the background and keeps track of everything the Record Panel does for sighted users (take counter, session name, scheduled recording and so on). Press F9 to arm the selected folder, again to start recording and again to stop. Hear the current input and status with the Mixer Mode announcement scripts, and use ! to repeat the last announcement. Set the session name, take number, scheduled start/end/duration, overlapping takes, horizontal takes and clip reporting in Accessible Recording Settings (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+R). When recording is finished, close the daemon with Close Recording Session (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F9). See Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader for setting up Clara.

Tip

There's no real need to position the edit cursor before starting to record as the arm/record function will automatically move the recording start position to after the final item in the armed folder.

Distributing Takes On Location

When you are recording on location, you can hand every take recorded so far to the musicians or the producer without leaving the session. Use Distribute Takes (Ctrl+Shift+D, called Quick Export Recorded Takes in the ReaClassical menu). It builds one region per take (for each folder, in either workflow) and renders each one through the mixer to the master as WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320, using the sample rate, bit depth and dither you choose for WAV and FLAC (Opus and MP3 keep their own fixed settings). The files go into a subfolder of Exports/Distribute_Takes named for the format and settings, so exporting again at a different rate or format never overwrites an earlier export. Folders other than the one being rendered are muted for each pass, and your mute states are restored afterwards.

Screen reader users (Clara)

Ctrl+Shift+D opens an accessible version with two rows, Render Settings (sample rate, bit depth, dither) and Export (choose the format and press Enter to render at once). It always exports every take; there is no track-range prompt.

Additional Notes on Record Panel

Session Names and Take Numbers

To set a session name, click the greyed "Session name" text beneath the take number in the Record Panel (only possible while stopped), type a name and press Enter (or click elsewhere). Press Esc to cancel. To remove the name, click it, delete the text with backspace and press Enter. Note that if you create a new session name, the take number will automatically be reset to 1. If you switch to an existing session name with recorded takes, the take number will be calculated accordingly.

Ranking and Notes

During recording, any ranking or notes added will affect the item created immediately after recording finishes. When transport is stopped, if no items are selected, ranking and notes affect the last recorded items. Apply ranking and notes to previous items in the timeline by selecting them.

Other Buttons and Options in the Main Window

Click the take number (after confirming) to recalculate the take count, and use the Settings button for the options described in Record Panel Settings. Use +Take (Shift+F9, also while recording) to quickly increase the take number (useful for a false start, for example). Press Next (Alt+F9) to start a new recording section. This means that in vertical workflow the first source folder is rec-armed and in both workflows, the edit cursor is placed 5 seconds after the final item in the project. Enable "Record Takes Horizontally" while in vertical workflow to record takes left to right on a single folder. This is useful, for example, if you prefer to have each folder contain takes for just one piece of music. In this instance, Next acts as a sort of carriage return and arms the next folder down as well as move the edit cursor to the start of the timeline (or after any existing material).

Record Panel Settings

Click the Settings button in the Record Panel to open a popup with the take number, scheduled recording and take placement options described below.

Allow Take Recording Anywhere

This setting overrides the default safety feature of only allowing new recorded items after the final item on the folder. This is useful if you record musical material out of order and wish to place new items at an arbitrary position on the project timeline.

Scheduled Recording

To start (and optionally end) a recording at specific times or manually start a recording to end at a certain time or after a certain duration, click the Settings button on the Record Panel window and add the appropriate entry or entries in HH:MM format. After pressing Apply, the Record Panel window will display information above the take number. If you enter a start or end time earlier or equal to the current time, the function will assume a next day schedule and will annotate the time with an asterisk (*). Likewise, with both a start and end time, if the end time is earlier than or equal to start, it will assume a time 24 hours later. Don't forget to arm your tracks before walking away!

Overriding Take Numbers

You shouldn't need to use this but there are cases where you might want to start a new ReaClassical project but continue from the previous day's last take number. To do so, check the "Allow Take Number Override" option and set a new take number. Note that it will not allow you to set a number lower than already used.

Remote Recording via web interface

The ReaClassical Remote is a browser-based control panel that mirrors the Record Panel's core functionality, allowing you to arm tracks, start and stop recording, manage takes, and apply rankings and notes from a phone, tablet, or laptop anywhere in the room. To set it up, enable REAPER's built-in web remote by opening REAPER preferences O and navigate to Control/OSC/web and add a new web browser interface from the drop-down. Select ReaClassical_remote.html from the default interface drop-down and click apply. This same options page displays a ready-made access URL. Simply open that in a browser on any device connected to the same local network. Once connected, the Arm/Rec/Stop button, Pause/Disarm, +Take, and Next Section buttons all behave identically to their counterparts in the Record Panel window, and the take number display is kept in sync with the running panel. Session settings including start and end times, duration, and session name are read from REAPER on first load and can be edited and applied back to the running panel from the Session Settings section at the bottom of the page. Rank and notes can be set remotely and will be applied to the last recorded items exactly as if you had used the Record Panel directly. Note that the Record Panel Lua script must be open and running for the remote to function correctly, as it acts as the bridge between the web interface and ReaClassical's project state.

Meterbridge

Use B to open the Meterbridge. The default view shows numeric peak holds. When tracks are record-armed, the main window displays recording inputs. During auditioning of material, the top rows show mixer tracks and the bottom any special tracks including RCMASTER and Master tracks. To switch to graphical meters, check the "Graphical Meters" option. Under the options tab, you can set color thresholds for yellow and red. To switch to channel numbers instead of hardware names, uncheck the option while tracks are rec-armed.

Recording Indicator

The recording indicator (Alt+R) is designed to be placed on a secondary monitor full screen so in situations where engineers are located in a separate control room, musicians are aware of when recording is active. Right-click to set custom colors for offline, standby, recording and pause.

Live Bounce

To record the rough balanced mix as a stereo file at the same time as individual channels, add a live bounce track via Mission Control. Note that this is only available in a horizontal workflow given the necessity to record left-to-right on the time line to align with the folder recording.

Listenback

To hear verbal feedback from a musician far away from the recording setup (for example, an organist in a loft), add a listenback track via Mission Control. Set the desired input channel via the dropdown. Monitoring will automatically mute during playback and recording. To set monitoring to always on, open the FX panel on the listenback track and set the dropdown in the monitoring JSFX to "Always On".

Splitting items into subtakes

To split a selected item into numbered subtakes, add generic markers via M at the desired locations and press Shift+S to split. To name a marker, press Alt+M (REAPER's insert and/or edit marker) and use the name instead of subtake numbering. Ctrl+M deletes the marker nearest the edit cursor, Ctrl+Shift+M moves the nearest marker to the edit cursor and Ctrl+Shift+G deletes all generic markers.

Monitoring and Playback

  • Toggle Monitor (Ctrl+Shift+A) cycles input monitoring on all the input tracks that are not disabled for recording: off, on, then tape mode. The new state is announced.
  • Toggle Playback (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P) mutes or unmutes the playback track (see Navigating a Project). The playback track is created muted, so this unmutes it for monitoring.
  • Take Number Display (Alt+T) shows the current take number in a small window. It is started automatically by the Record Panel Daemon in the screen reader recording workflow, so that a sighted colleague can see the current take.

Headroom

REAPER's peak indicators are reset automatically each time recording starts, so the peak values you see afterwards belong to the current take. Again, I refer you to the books on classical music production but in general I suggest aiming for around -12dB peaks on the meters. 24-bit recording allows for a lot of headroom so there's no need to push close to 0dB. Adjust the individual mixer track faders to balance. When using a 32-bit float device with dual AD converters as an interface (such as the Zoom F-series), ensure that the recording file format is switched to 32-bit float via project preferences P. The recorded levels might seem too low or too high during recording, but they can be easily adjusted afterward in ReaClassical without introducing any extra noise or distortion.

Recording Safety

When using the Record Panel for recording (essential!), there is increased safety when using classical take recording via the automatic switch to a restricted set of keyboard shortcuts. In addition to using the record panel, you can also access various non-disruptive functions like zooming.

Overdub Recording

To record additional material after the fact (say a separate narration track or an organ part in a church after the main recording session in a concert hall), edit the orchestral material as usual and use a mixdown as a guide track in a new project (or new project tab). To achieve this, use a vertical workflow (convert if necessary via Mission Control C), add a Reference track also via Mission Control and set the ReaClassical Project Preferences option REF = Overdub Guide to checked (F5). With this setting, audio on the guide track will be audible during take recording and auditioning of folders. Use Classical Take Recording via the Record Panel as normal. You can then S-D edit and mix the overdub material to fit with the orchestral mixdown or, if further mixing and mastering work is required on the original multi-track material, bring the organ part into that project as a new track in the folders (see below).

Manipulating Tracks During a Recording Session

Screen reader users (Clara)

Use Accessible Track Setup to add, delete and reorder tracks (including aux and submix tracks) from the keyboard instead of Mission Control.

Disabling Channels

In a typical recording session, the musicians with the least to record are often allowed to leave the session early once their work is completed. If they were individually recorded using a spot microphone, it wouldn't make sense to continue recording on that channel. The ReaClassical way, both easy and visually obvious, is to open Mission Control C and check "Rec Disabled" for the particular channel(s). When arming and recording, these channels will now be excluded. This allows the user to maintain hardware connections that were originally set up with the ability to quickly bring the microphone back in as required.

Adding a New Microphone Mid-Recording Session

You can add a track to all folders in the project at once via Mission Control. It will prompt you for a name and then add a new track with that name to the end of each folder. This also works for a single folder while working in a horizontal workflow.

Deleting tracks

In both horizontal and vertical workflows, you can use Mission Control to quickly delete child tracks from all folders of the project.

Re-ordering tracks

In both horizontal and vertical workflows, you can re-order the mixer tracks by selecting the track in Mission Control and using the arrow buttons. This also moves all audio and assigned recording inputs. Aux and submix tracks can be moved up and down in the same way.

Audio Calculator

To figure out required disk space for a duration of audio or vice versa to figure out maximum duration of audio you can record based on available disk space, use Shift+H to open a calculator. You can set units, channel count, samplerate, bit depth and format (WAV or MP3 at various bitrates).

Screen reader users (Clara)

The Accessible Audio Calculator offers the same calculation as a keyboard-driven window.

Importing

While it is always better to record in ReaClassical for traditional recording sessions, you may prefer using a portable recorder for live performances. Further, you might need to import audio recorded by other engineers who used a different DAW.

Smart Import

Smart Import brings in audio files that follow a simple naming scheme, working out the track, take and (optionally) session from the filename. It handles both ordinary mono and stereo files and multi-channel files from portable recorders (see Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder).

File Naming

The take number must be at the very end of the filename, just before the extension, preceded by an underscore. The "T" (for take) and any zero-padding are optional. The part of the name before the take number is split at underscores: the last part is the track name and anything before it is the session name. Examples (where x represents a digit):

  • sessionname_trackname_Txxx.wav
  • sessionname_trackname_xxx.wav
  • trackname_Txx.wav
  • trackname_xxx.wav

Examples of good filenaming include:

  • morning_cello_012.wav (session "morning", track name will match "cello", take 12)
  • day1_morning_cello_012.wav (session "day1_morning", track name will match "cello", take 12)
  • harpsichord_T4.flac (no session name, track name will match "harpsichord", take 4)

Examples of bad filenaming include:

  • 005.wav (no track name)
  • violin56.wav (no underscore before the take number)

WAV, FLAC and AIFF files are imported. A file named roomtone.wav is always ignored, as it is reserved for room tone.

Important

Don't skip this renaming step if you want to import files easily from another DAW! Manual import by dragging in material can be time-consuming and may not allow you to use functions like searching by take number.

Importing

  1. Ensure that you have first created a horizontal or vertical workflow ReaClassical project.
  2. Copy or move source material into the media subfolder inside your ReaClassical project folder (you can also assign a custom import/recording path via Project Settings P). Subfolders are searched too.
  3. Either leave the track names blank (recommended) or ensure that track names in the project match the track text in the filenames. If your filenames also contain a session name prior to the track name, the items will be grouped accordingly.
  4. Via the top ReaClassical menu, click on Project Management > Smart Import Audio or use shortcut Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I.
  5. Choose your options on the Named Tracks tab and press Import.
  6. Open Mission Control to add special tracks such as aux & submix, make routing adjustments etc.

The Named Tracks tab shows the workflow of the project, how many new takes and sessions were found, and where the material will be inserted. Files already used in the project are ignored, so you can "smart" import further material into a non-empty ReaClassical project.

Material is inserted at the edit cursor. The import is built first and then, if anything already sits at or after the cursor on the folders being imported into, that material is moved later by exactly the length of the import to make room. Only the folders that actually receive imported items are affected: importing into the first source folder does not disturb the destination folder or untouched source folders. If an existing item straddles the cursor, it and everything after it move, and a one-second gap is left after the new material.

If the project's track names are all blank, you are first given the opportunity to set the order in which the captured track names are assigned to the mixer tracks by dragging rows into place.

Import only these takes (optional) lets you restrict an import to a session name and/or a list of takes such as 1-3,5,11-15.

In a horizontal workflow all takes are laid out left to right in the single folder, one session after another.

In a vertical workflow, takes are placed in source folders. Choose the Starting folder (the first source folder to use) and a Distribution Mode:

  • One folder per take: within each session, the first take goes in the starting folder, the second in the next folder down, and so on. New source folders are created if the project doesn't have enough. Each further session begins again at the starting folder, to the right of the previous one.
  • Use current folder count: takes are dealt out in turn across all the source folders that already exist from the starting folder downward (take 1 to the first, take 2 to the second, ..., then back to the first folder, to the right of the first round). No folders are created.
  • Round-robin across custom number of folders: the same dealing out, but across the number of folders you enter, creating folders if needed.

A preview shows the result, including a warning when new folders will be created.

Screen reader users (Clara)

The same shortcut opens a keyboard-driven walkthrough, announced through Clara, with an explicit confirmation step before the import happens. If the media folder also contains multi-channel files, you are first asked to choose between Import Takes and Import Polywav.

Multi-Channel Files from a Portable Recorder

If you use a portable recorder such as a MixPre, you might have a multi-channel combined file (a "polywav"). Smart Import can split these into a set of mono and stereo tracks. The Polywav tab appears in the Smart Import window whenever the media folder contains unused files with more than two channels.

The filenames must follow the take-number rule above, with an optional session name but no track name: [sessionname_]Txxx.wav. Every polywav imported in one go must have the same number of channels.

Enter a channel composition pattern made of the digits 1 (mono) and 2 (stereo), read left to right across the channels of the file. For example:

  • 2 makes the first stereo pair, and then every remaining pair of channels is also treated as stereo
  • 21 makes a stereo pair followed by a mono channel; the remaining channels are mono
  • 221 makes two stereo pairs followed by mono channels for everything else

Once the digits have been used up, the last digit repeats for as many whole groups as still fit, and anything left over becomes mono tracks. ReaClassical checks that the result fits before touching your project, then distributes the takes with the same options as Named Tracks.

The channel groups are placed on the tracks of the folder in order: the first group goes to the first track, the second to the second, and so on, so the project needs at least as many tracks per folder as there are groups. Tracks that already have names keep them, so you can set up your tracks first and the channels simply follow their order. Any blank tracks are named after their channels (for example "Ch 1" or "Ch 2-3 (Stereo)"). The Polywav tab works on its own, so a media folder that contains only multi-channel files is fine.

Importing a DDP or PMI

ReaClassical can rebuild a full CD track and album metadata layout from an existing master, for checking or remastering. Use a fresh ReaClassical project whose destination folder is empty.

  • Project Management > Import DDP (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+D): choose the DDP's raw audio stream, a file with a .DAT extension (conventionally IMAGE.DAT)
  • Project Management > Import PMI (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M): choose a Pyramix .pmi pre-master

Manual Import by Dragging

  1. In your source folder, select items that should be aligned vertically (for example, every channel for particular take) and drag into the ReaClassical project being sure to drop onto one of the folders created by ReaClassical with a track count that matches the number of files you selected. Choose the option "Same time position on separate tracks"
  2. Continue as above for each take
  3. Open Mission Control C to add special tracks such as aux & submix, make routing adjustments etc.

Navigating a Project

In addition to built-in REAPER functions, ReaClassical uses a series of keyboard shortcuts to help you easily navigate your classical project. You can of course still navigate by clicking around with the mouse as you would in any REAPER project; the shortcuts are there to make it faster, and to make it possible without the mouse at all. Important: I always make some dedicated time post-recording to get an overview of the recorded material, tidy up the digital notes I took during the session and perform a backup on an external drive as soon as possible.

Whole Project

Use Ctrl+Alt+→ (or Ctrl+Alt+←) to see the whole project horizontally and/or Ctrl+Alt+↓ (or Ctrl+Alt+↑) to see everything vertically. If you want to zoom both horizontally and vertically at the same time, use ` (backtick). REAPER's own Home and End keys take you to the start or end of the project. + and - zoom in and out horizontally.

Tracks and Folders

The arrow keys move you around the project without the mouse. Each move selects the track and announces it (name, peak level and any mute or solo state):

  • ↓ and ↑: next and previous track within the current folder. In a project with a single track per folder these move between folders instead
  • Alt+↓ and Alt+↑: next and previous folder
  • D: the first folder in the project

Moving to a folder makes it the folder you hear (the others are muted) and selects the item nearest the edit cursor. If a special track such as an aux, submix or reference is selected, ↓ and ↑ step through the visible special tracks instead. To jump straight to a track by name, press Shift+J and type part of its name.

Finding Takes

Use Enter on the main keyboard or numpad to quickly search for a take based on the underlying filename of the media item. This will work for any file-naming system that uses numbers before the file extension such as mainpair-T04.wav, cello-spot-take23.flac or even ortfpair(04).wav such as created by Presonus Studio One. Note that if the imported or recorded files have zero-padding that is not a problem. If you have used an item to create an S-D edit, searching for a take will ignore these items and move directly to the original sources. In F5 preferences, you can set to search by item name instead. In the ReaClassical Notes app N, you can override and reset take numbers. These take priority in the search.

Jump to Time

Press J to jump to a specific absolute or relative time using right-aligned logic, similar to video editing applications. Press Ctrl+J to do the same within the selected item or a set of consecutive crossfaded items, where an absolute time counts from the start of that selection. Prefix with + or - to make relative jumps from the current cursor position. Colons are ignored, so 1:23:45:10 and 01234510 are read the same way. Once you get the hang of using this input logic, moving to any position is extremely quick!

Some Right-Aligned Logic Examples

Input Meaning (based on project frame rate)
100524 Move to absolute position 10m 5s 24f
1141711 Move to absolute position 1h 14m 17s 11f
+8 Jump forward by 8 frames
-1015 Jump backward by 10s 15f
+23000 Jump forward by 2m 30s (and 0 frames)

Items & Markers

You can shuffle back and forth between item edges and fades by using ← and → (or Q and W). While editing a crossfade these move through the crossfade, and with an envelope selected they move between its points. More precise item moves:

  • Alt+← and Alt+→: start and end of the selected item
  • Ctrl+Shift+← and Ctrl+Shift+→: first and last item on the track
  • Shift+Q and Shift+W: start and end of the folder
  • Alt+Q and Alt+W: previous and next group of crossfaded items

Move between markers by using the , and . keys (by design given on my keyboard they are the same keys that have < and >).

Markers, Regions and Time Selection

  • M adds a marker at the cursor and Alt+M inserts or edits a marker (to give it a name). Ctrl+M deletes the marker nearest the cursor, Ctrl+Shift+M moves the nearest marker to the cursor, Ctrl+Shift+G deletes all generic markers and L opens REAPER's region and marker manager. S-D markers use their own keys; see Editing
  • ; creates a region from each selected item, named after the active take, : creates a region from the time selection, and Ctrl+Alt+R deletes all regions
  • [ and ] set the start and end of the time selection at the cursor, Ctrl+] and Ctrl+[ move the cursor to the start and end of the time selection, and / sets the time selection to the selected items
  • 0 deselects all items

Parents & Children

ReaClassical can hide or show children of track folders. This means that editing multi-track classical music can be as easy as editing a stereo track. Making an edit to the parent track automatically makes the same one to all the children too. To show or hide the children, select the parent track and press E. The other benefit is that a whole set of takes can be displayed vertically in the main editing window without too much effort.

Peaks Display

To adjust the visual zoom of wave peaks, use Ctrl+↑ and Ctrl+↓. This is purely visual and allows for easier editing of quieter sections.

ReaClassical S-D Editing Toolbar

While I designed ReaClassical to be used efficiently with keyboard shortcuts, there is a custom S-D editing toolbar for those that prefer it. However I do highly recommend learning the key strokes as you will find your editing speeds improve dramatically. The floating toolbar can be opened via F6 but will automatically open once when you start source-destination editing. Right-click to set a different icon layout and/or zoom. Hover over the icons to discover what is available.

ReaClassical Top Menu

At the top of the arrange window, you will see a dedicated ReaClassical menu (in between Options and Extensions). While not intended to be used as the primary way of running ReaClassical functions, it is an organized way of discovering the individual available functions and learning the keyboard shortcuts.

Screen reader users (Clara)

Every navigation move above is announced, so no extra step is needed. Use Shift+J to go straight to a track by name, and ! to hear the last announcement again. The announcement shortcuts for take number, timeline position and items in the folder are listed in Using ReaClassical with a Screen Reader.

Summary of Track Types in ReaClassical

While some of these will be covered later in the manual, it is useful to give a summary of track types you can currently use in ReaClassical. First, we have the regular folder or folder of tracks shown in the arrange window. These are where you record or import takes. Second, we have the mixer tracks designated via M: prefix. These tracks shown only in the mixer are where you adjust the usual track controls such as names, pan, volume, phase, add FX etc. Their names are synced across the project via when added or renamed via Mission Control. Third, we have aux busses designated via @ prefix. You can route mixer tracks to these to use as a reverb bus etc. Fourth, we have submix busses designated via # prefix. You can route mixer tracks to these as a way to collect together microphones from the same orchestral section etc. Fifth, we have a dedicated room tone track where you can place recorded or generated room tone (more on this in the mastering section). Sixth, we have the RCMASTER bus which leads directly to the master REAPER bus. Here you can gain stage into the master bus, add FX etc. Seventh, we have reference tracks which lie outside of the RCMASTER structure thereby allowing the user to quickly make comparisons with other imported material via the audition shortcuts. Next, there is the possibility of a live bounce track. This also lies outside of the RCMASTER structure and is a way to capture a live stereo mix from the RCMASTER track.

Note

Live bounce tracks are only available when recording in a horizontal workflow.

Next, another track outside of the RCMASTER structure is the listenback track. This is a way to monitor musicians, conductors, producers etc who might be far away and need to communicate with the recording engineer via a microphone channel. There is also a playback track (a maximum of one, shown in the mixer only, created muted) that you can send to a chosen pair of hardware outputs and unmute for monitoring with Ctrl+Alt+Shift+P. Finally, the master bus itself where again you can set final levels, add FX etc. As mentioned elsewhere, try not to delete the mixer tracks or RCMASTER. But, even if you do by accident, open Mission Control C to recreate them.

Important

A reminder to do all track management in Mission Control!

Project Management

Statistics

For a complete set of statistics on the ReaClassical project, either for your own information or to assist with billing a client, go to ReaClassical > Utilities > Show Statistics or use the shortcut F1. For example, you might have a billing system that charges clients based on number of source-destination edits, or mixing/mastering based on the final length of the album. Information includes:

  • Album: final album length, number of CD markers, and the number of items and total length of material outside the album (anything on the first track after a gap of more than 60 seconds; see the tip at the start of the Mastering chapter)
  • Project: project age, session time, total project length, total length of source material, total number of items, number of track folders, number of tracks per folder, number of special tracks and number of regions
  • Edits: number of destination S-D edits and destination item splits
  • FX and automation: total FX count and number of automation lanes

Session time is the elapsed time (in hours and minutes) since the project's session timer was started, and can be reset to zero from the statistics window. The window also shows your ReaClassical and REAPER versions. The statistics can be copied to the clipboard.

Screen reader users (Clara)

With Clara installed, F1 opens Accessible Show Statistics, which lists the same values for you to step through and lets you reset the session timer.

Typing Notes

Add project, track and item notes using ReaClassical's Notes window (N, or ReaClassical > Utilities > Add Project/Track/Item Notes). For the selected item you can also set the item name, item rank and take number (with a button to reset it to the number found in the filename), as well as an item note. The take number you set here takes priority when finding takes.

Screen reader users (Clara)

N opens an accessible Notes window with the same fields. Use Left/Right (or Q/W) to move between items while it is open and Space to play and stop. Item Rank (Ctrl+R) and Item Name (Shift+N) also have their own quick windows.

Manually Coloring Items

Use the Colorize function (K, or Colorize Selected Item(s) in the ReaClassical menu) to set a custom color (or remove it) for the selected items.

Folder Structure

ReaClassical defaults to placing recorded media in a media subfolder and exports in an Exports subfolder of the project folder, making project file navigation easier.

Automatic Backups

REAPER allows for powerful and complex backup routines. ReaClassical sets REAPER's auto-save to every 15 minutes and keeps a limited number of backups. Review and modify these in REAPER's Preferences under Project > Backups to suit your own way of working, including switching to backups and auto saves for a number of unique days.

Folders and Items

  • Duplicate folder (No items) (Ctrl+D) adds a copy of the selected folder's tracks as a new folder, without its items. From a horizontal workflow it first asks whether to convert to a vertical workflow
  • Delete Source Folder (Shift+D) deletes the selected source folder (vertical workflow only; it asks you to confirm)
  • Delete All Source Items (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Delete) deletes every item in every source folder (vertical workflow only; it asks you to confirm)
  • Select All Items in Folder (Ctrl+Alt+A) selects every item in the folder of the selected track
  • Paste (Ctrl+V) pastes items and announces how many were pasted
  • Remove All Item Fades (Shift+F) removes the fades from items whose edges are not part of a crossfade, leaving crossfades intact

Project Tabs

Ctrl+Alt+N opens a new project tab and Ctrl+Tab (or NumPad +) switches to the next one. Switching announces the name of the project you land on. Multiple project tabs are the way to make multi-disc albums and to compile edits from several projects; see Multi-Project Tab S-D Editing.

Cleaning

If in doubt, keep everything! Otherwise, the File > Clean current project directory is an excellent way to reduce the size of your projects. Note that when assigning a session name via the Record Panel Window, currently the above REAPER menu item doesn't search recursively. In a way, this reduces the chances of accidentally deleting precious takes. You can always manually delete but, from experience, it is much better to simply keep everything.

Archiving

There are various ways to archive classical music projects. First, you can access the Project Bay by Ctrl+B shortcut. You can then ensure that all media used in the project is contained within the project folder itself. If not, you can select as many as necessary, right click and move/copy into the project folder. After this, you can simply compress the folder as a zip and store on an external drive. A further step to guaranteeing ability to open in the future is to freeze tracks so that plugin effects are baked in (with ability to unfreeze later if possible). Alternatively you can save a copy of the project via File > Save project as..., converting to a format like FLAC and trimming the media as you wish. Finally, one to look out for in the future is Project Archiver. However, I don't believe it is quite ready for prime-time yet and recommend using one of the other methods for now.

Auditioning

Auditioning Folders

Audition your material via mouse hover + A on parent or child tracks. The folder under the mouse becomes the one you hear (the others are muted), any record-armed tracks are disarmed, and playback starts from the mouse position. Use hover + Shift+A to play back at a custom rate set via ReaClassical Preferences F5 (default x0.75). Use mixer mute and solo buttons to further customize what you hear. Hover over a reference track for easy A/Bing between your audio production and one or more reference audio files.

Tip

To quickly remove all record-arming in the project, use mouse hover + A or close the Record Panel.

Choosing the Folder from the Keyboard

You do not need the mouse to choose which folder you hear. Moving to a folder with Alt+↓, Alt+↑ or D (see Navigating a Project) makes it the audible folder, and Space plays and stops. Shift+Space plays and stops while moving the edit cursor with the playhead, and Ctrl+Shift+Space returns to the position where you last stopped.

Auditioning Around S-D Markers

Once you have set source and destination markers, you can hear them without moving the cursor. Each shortcut selects the relevant folder, makes it audible and plays a short segment:

Shortcut Plays
6 / 8 3 seconds from the destination IN / OUT marker
7 / 9 3 seconds from the source IN / OUT marker
Ctrl+6 / Ctrl+8 the 3 seconds up to the destination IN / OUT marker
Ctrl+7 / Ctrl+9 the 3 seconds up to the source IN / OUT marker
Alt+6 or Alt+8 from the destination IN marker to the destination OUT marker
Alt+7 or Alt+9 from the source IN marker to the source OUT marker

If a required marker is missing, ReaClassical says so. Starting a new audition stops any audition still playing. To compare takes before choosing source markers, see the Source Audition Manager (Z) in the Editing chapter.

Screen reader users (Clara)

All of these work with the keyboard alone and announce what they are doing, including a message when a marker is missing or when the OUT marker is not after the IN marker.

  • ← Previous
  • ↑ Up

Editing

Source-destination editing is truly anywhere to anywhere. This means you can place your source and destination marker pairs on any folder.

Editing Step-by-Step

Ensure that the folder where you want to place the marker pair is selected. The best way to do this is to click on the item where you want the marker. Note that in F5 preferences you can set placement at mouse hover meaning that the desired folder is chosen based on hover position.

  1. Set destination IN and OUT markers via 1 and 2
  2. Set source IN and OUT markers via 3 and 4
  3. Press 5 to make the source-destination edit (2-, 3- or 4-point edit depending on how many markers you set), or F4 to make a time-stretched S-D edit (requires all 4 markers), or if only using destination IN marker and both source markers, F3 for an "assembly" or 3-point "insert" edit
  4. To finesse the edit, click on the right item of a crossfade pair and press F

Screen reader users (Clara)

Every marker and edit action announces what it did. If you place a marker on the wrong side of its partner (a source OUT before the existing source IN, for example), ReaClassical deletes the stale marker and says so, so an edit can never silently take far more material than you intended. Use Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+4 to move to each marker and the audition keys described in Auditioning to hear them. For crossfades, see Crossfade Editing for Screen Reader Users.

Coloring and Fixing Takes

There is no separate "prepare takes" step before editing any more. ReaClassical's editing functions find the matching items on the other tracks of a folder by midpoint matching rather than relying on explicit group IDs, and empty items are cleared out automatically each time Mission Control opens.

  • Auto-color project (Shift+K) colors items by take number or folder. ReaClassical runs it for you at the points where it is needed; run it yourself after importing material by hand. Set No Auto Item Coloring in the F5 preferences to switch it off.
  • Fix Crossfade Sequence Edits (Shift+X) repairs items that should be grouped but have become misaligned across the tracks of a folder, for example because ripple-per-track was switched off by accident while dragging items. Select any one of them, run it and choose which track has the correct edits. Every other track in the folder is rebuilt across that group from the reference track's edits, re-pointed at each track's own audio file for the same take number.

Crossfade Editor

Since v7.40, REAPER includes an excellent professional two-lane crossfade editor similar in nature to the specialist classical DAWs such as Sequoia and Pyramix. With the improved crossfade editor, users can see the continued "ghost" waveforms of the items beyond the crossfade they enter and likewise the previous waveforms of the items that exit the crossfade. The ability to visually align transients and then position the crossfade just before it is absolutely critical (and fun when you have the tools to do it!). Select the right-hand item of a fade (or hover over the item if Add S-D Markers at Mouse Hover is set in the F5 preferences) and press F to enter crossfade editor mode. Press F again to leave it. The two-lane editor has its own keyboard shortcuts for auditioning and navigating. To audition material, hover the mouse inside the crossfade window and:

  • Press A to audition the crossfade with mirrored pre/post roll based on mouse cursor location
  • Press S to audition just the left item based on mouse cursor location or its mirrored position
  • Press D to audition just the right item based on mouse cursor location or its mirrored position

Use Shift+A, Shift+S or Shift+D to do the equivalent but with a custom playrate as set in F5 preferences. Other shortcuts include:

  • Press E to audition just the top lane based on mouse cursor location or its mirrored position
  • Press C to audition just the bottom lane based on mouse cursor location or its mirrored position
  • Press Alt+S to audition just the out-of-bounds material left of the xfade
  • Press Alt+D to audition just the out-of-bounds material right of the xfade

You can shuttle between crossfades using the Q and W shortcuts (or ← and →). Please see the REAPER manual for more details of what is possible including phase alignment and various view options.

Crossfade Editing for Screen Reader Users

Screen reader users (Clara)

REAPER's two-lane crossfade editor depends on seeing and dragging the waveforms, so it is not usable with a screen reader. With Clara installed, F starts a keyboard-driven crossfade mode instead, which gives you the same control over the crossfade: nothing is lost. See Crossfade Mode for all of its keys.

Source Audition Manager

When making a source-destination edit, you may not have a list or annotated score from the musicians or producer showing preferred edits. If the decision is left to the audio engineer, this process is very straightforward. First set the source audition mode to checked in F5 preferences. Then, open the Source Audition Manager via the Source Audition button in Mission Control or the Z shortcut. To set up all the source audition pairs, set multiple sets of source in and out markers. You will note that when you start to add a second pair, the source markers are transformed into a take marker "region". The only limitation is that you can only have a single take marker region set per item. This allows the user to quickly reposition the S-D markers by simply setting new ones. If your recorded items each contain multiple passes of the same musical material, consider splitting them via the S shortcut. Use the controls in the window to audition, rank and add notes. Once you have settled on a best take, press the convert button (or place edit cursor within a take marker region and press Alt+Z). Note, that any existing real source pair is converted to a take marker region. Assuming one or more destination markers are already set, you can press 5, F3 or F4 to make the desired edit. Sometimes the suitability of source material is difficult to judge until it is heard with the surrounding destination material. Given that all source markers are stored as take marker regions if inactive, it allows the user to quickly undo an edit and switch to an alternative pair. During auditioning, you can delete individual pairs via the X on the specific table row, as well as delete all source audition markers by clicking Delete All Audition Markers or pressing Alt+Delete.

Other Editing Tips

Making a Crossfade by Hand

If two items on a parent track overlap, place the edit cursor somewhere within the overlap and press X to crossfade them. The crossfade uses the S-D Crossfade Length from the F5 preferences (35 ms by default) and is applied to every track in the folder. You can then refine it in the crossfade editor with F.

Healing Edits

Select any S-D edit and press Ctrl+H to heal it, restoring the material the edit replaced. This works for every kind of S-D edit (3-point insert, 4-point, and 4-point with timestretching), including edits where the material either side of the edit comes from different takes. ReaClassical saves the underlying material at the moment you make the edit, so there is no need for the surrounding items to match.

If the edit is made up of several items (for example because the source section spans more than one source item), selecting any one of them heals the whole edit.

Tip

This works at any point in the editing process and isn't restricted to the last edit made.

Note

Edits made with earlier versions of ReaClassical have no saved material. These can still be healed only when the items either side of the edit come from the same source file, with the later item further along in that file (for example, a patch over the top of a single best take). If an edit has since been changed in a way that no longer matches what was saved (such as splitting one of its items), ReaClassical falls back to the same rule. Healing an edit that has another edit directly alongside it is best done in reverse order: heal the most recent edit first.

Finding Source Material

The items representing a S-D edit are colored according to the source material. However, you can also easily locate source material by clicking on an edited item and pressing Ctrl+F. A color-coordinated source IN and OUT marker pair are placed at the source location and in vertical workflow mode, the associated folder is selected. This function also works across multiple project tabs.

Set Item Playrate with Ripple

This function, run via Shift+R, allows you to change the playback rate of a selected item, automatically rippling all subsequent items within the same folder to maintain the integrity of your edits. Select a single item on the folder track, enter a percentage value in the input box, and press Apply & Ripple. In relative mode (the default), the value is applied as a percentage change relative to the item's current rate — so entering 5 makes the item 5% faster than it currently is, while -5 makes it 5% slower. In absolute mode (enable the "Absolute rate" checkbox), the value is always relative to normal speed — so 5 always results in a rate of 1.05x regardless of the item's current rate, and 0 always restores normal speed. The Reset to Normal Speed button is a convenient shortcut to return the item to 1.0x playback rate. Pitch is always preserved during time-stretching. Note that only one item may be selected at a time, as each item requires its own independent ripple calculation. The window also includes a Pitch Adjustment section for correcting intonation without affecting item length or requiring any ripple. Enter a value in semitones and press Apply Pitch — positive values raise the pitch, negative values lower it, and fractional values are supported for fine adjustments (e.g. 0.5 for a quarter-tone). The Reset Pitch button returns the pitch to 0.0 (no adjustment).

Screen reader users (Clara)

With Clara installed, Shift+R opens the accessible Playback Rate window, a keyboard walkthrough that makes the same rate and pitch changes with the same rippling. Press H in it for examples that fit the current relative or absolute mode.

Automatic Crossfade Protection

When performing S-D edits, deletions or ripple deletes, ReaClassical automatically detects any existing crossfades that straddle your marker boundaries and consumes them as part of the resulting edit. This prevents stray partial fades being left behind in your project. This is also useful when quickly iterating through alternative source material: since destination markers persist after an edit and are placed at the exact edit bounds, you can create new source markers and immediately re-edit without worrying about crossfade debris accumulating at the destination boundaries.

Marking Edits on your Scores

This is best done using a physical, photocopied score by the conductor or lead musician. I advocate for a “T” system where a large T is inserted into the score at the intended edit point. Either side of the T stem, and under the crossbar, the outgoing and incoming take numbers are written. A wavy crossbar indicates some leeway for where the edit point can be placed. Further notes can be attached underneath the T such as directions for tightening the gap etc.

Multi-Project Tab S-D Editing

If you'd like to S-D edit between various open project tabs you can set both the source and destination project markers via Ctrl+Alt+1 (or Ctrl+Alt+2) for destination and Ctrl+Alt+3 (or Ctrl+Alt+4) for source (essentially the same numbers associated with regular S-D markers). The markers can exist anywhere on the tab's timeline but perhaps the very beginning or end would be good to keep them out of the way. The S-D editing itself then works just as for a single tab other than any source markers that are set are not deleted to aid quickly undoing in the destination tab and being ready to reapply the edit. The only rule when using S-D project markers is to ensure that source or destination markers should be paired with the corresponding source or destination project marker. This workflow would, for example, allow you to have multiple project tabs (perhaps one for each symphony movement plus a final destination tab), allowing for both internal editing per tab but after setting the S-D project markers compiling the final edit in the destination tab. To delete all the S-D project markers press Shift+Delete. Also, in multi-tab S-D editing, when regular markers are placed, any other existing versions in other tabs are automatically deleted to ensure that only one version of the marker exists at a time across all open project tabs.

Delete / Delete with Ripple

While perhaps not used as often as 3- and 4-point edits, I have created two functions for deletion of material. Delete & Ripple Backspace will delete the material between source IN and OUT markers and ripple material to the right backwards with a short crossfade. Delete Leaving Silence Ctrl+Backspace will also delete but maintain the silence without rippling backwards.

Copy/Move Destination Material to Source

Run either the copy Ctrl+Alt+C or move Ctrl+Alt+M version of the function from the S-D editing toolbar (no need to ensure the first track is selected) and the function will copy or move all items and edits from the destination folder directly below to a newly created source folder. This allows for saving versions of finished edits either via iteration (copying so you can continue to make further edits) or fresh (moving so you can compile an alternate version of a best take from scratch). These different edits can then be easily auditioned via A the shortcut. This is similar to a Pyramix-style iterative editing method while still maintaining the destination folder as the uppermost folder.

Promote Source to Destination

Select a source folder and press the "promote" icon in the S-D editing toolbar or Ctrl+Alt+P to promote the source folder to the top "destination" position.

Add S-D Markers to Edges of Item(s) or Time Selection

Used in combination with Delete / Delete with Ripple (Ctrl+Backspace/Backspace), you can quickly set both source markers to the edges of one or more selected items on a parent track or time selection via F12. This is a time-saver when dealing with potential sliver edits i.e. small unneeded leftover edits as a result of multiple rounds of zoomed-out S-D editing. Note that the built-in checks when manually placing destination markers should go some way to alleviating this issue which can easily go unnoticed in other classical music DAWs. Likewise you can use Ctrl+F12 to set destination markers (selected items must be in the destination folder). Note that if using time selection for placing source markers, as for S-D marker placement via 3 or 4, make sure you first have the desired source folder track selected before pressing the shortcut (a good way to do this is to first click on the item involved). You may prefer to set both source and destination markers this way over the more traditional number key shortcuts acting as a sort of hybrid between S-D and razor editing. Also note that if both selected items and a time selection exist, the time selection takes precedence.

Nudging Markers and Items

After auditioning a marker, nudge it with Ctrl+, (left) and Ctrl+. (right). Selected items are nudged with Alt+, and Alt+.. Both move by the project nudge amount, which you set with the Terminal command nudge=10 (milliseconds) or under Other Settings in Accessible Preferences. The same keys with the "x modifier" (Ctrl+Alt+, and Ctrl+Alt+. for markers, Alt+< and Alt+> for items) move by the nudge amount multiplied by the modifier amount (Terminal mod=10). Each nudge is announced with the item name and the distance moved. While a crossfade is being edited in crossfade mode, use the crossfade mode nudge keys instead.

Move / Zoom to S-D markers

To move to any existing S-D markers use Ctrl+1, Ctrl+2, Ctrl+3 or Ctrl+4. To zoom to any of the S-D markers for more fine-grained placement, use Alt+1, Alt+2, Alt+3 or Alt+4. If you have multi-tab S-D editing set up, these shortcuts will also automatically move focus to the correct project tab.

Delete S-D markers

To delete all regular S-D markers, press Ctrl+Delete.

Floating Destination Folder

The floating destination folder feature enhances vertical workflow efficiency by dynamically positioning the destination folder just above the selected source folder. This reduces unnecessary vertical scrolling when setting IN and OUT markers for destination and source folders that are far apart in the project. Additionally, this feature is fully compatible with mouse hover S-D editing and when setting source markers to item edges (F12). To enable the floating destination folder, open ReaClassical Project Preferences (F5) and set the corresponding line to checked. For example, with floating destination enabled, place a source IN marker (via 3) on any source folder. The destination folder will reposition itself just above the selected source folder. Add the remaining S-D markers as required. Perform any S-D edits via 5, F4, or F3. Select another source parent and place another marker (3). The destination folder will continue adjusting dynamically. It is worth noting that if the destination folder moves above a source folder, the source marker track number correctly updates to reflect the new order. To disable floating mode, re-open ReaClassical Project Preferences and set Floating Destination Folder unchecked. This will also automatically move the destination folder back to the top of the project.

Razor Editing

Because of the potential for visual overlap of markers, I much prefer the REAPER razor edit functionality for vertical take work. It works a lot like the process shown in this Pyramix video. While Pyramix also has additional source-destination marker workflows, I couldn't help but feel that for professional ensembles that manage a high degree of tempo regularity between takes, this method can be extremely efficient. This isn't the document to introduce REAPER razor edits as there are plenty of resources online if you do a simple search. Here we are only concerning ourselves with creation of the razor area across all our pairs and spot mics (REAPER's default shortcut is the rather uninspiring Alt+Right drag). Thankfully, it can become the default editing mode by selecting the razor edit mode on the main toolbar and left-click dragging.

Mixing

Mixing Scenes

  1. Add FX, change routing, and optionally adjust volume, panning etc via Mission Control C
  2. Open Mixer Snapshot Manager via Shift+M
  3. Create automatically-recalled mixer snapshots tied to items.
  4. Before rendering, convert to real automation lanes via Convert to Automation

Note

If setting a snapshot tied to an unnamed item, the first part of the item's ID will be used as the identifier in the table row.

Mixer Snapshot Manager in Detail

General Workflow

  1. Click on an item that you want to be the start of a snapshot or mixer "scene"
  2. Adjust any mixer parameter including fader, mute/solo, pan, FX parameters etc
  3. Click Set Snapshot....
  4. To make changes, select the item or table row, tweak parameters and click the same button now re-labeled Update Snapshot...

By default, switching mixer scenes will happen in a gap in the project during playback. Disable auto recall to treat as a simple mixer snapshot tool that affects the whole project. Filter which parameters are recalled by unchecking boxes at the bottom of the window: volume, pan, mute, solo, phase, width, FX, send levels and send routing. By default a snapshot takes effect in the middle of the gap between items; uncheck Switch mid-gap during playback to switch only at the start of the next item that has a snapshot.

Snapshots can only be set on items on the first (destination) folder track, which is the track that recall and gap detection are based on.

Important

Auto recall runs while the Mixer Snapshot Manager is open. To keep it running after you close the window, check Background auto-recall, which hands recall over to a background process. Once converted to real automation points, auto recall is disabled by design and the window can be closed.

Screen reader users (Clara)

Select an item on the first folder and press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+S (Snapshot Add) to capture a snapshot, or press Shift+M, which opens the accessible Snapshot Settings in place of the Mixer Snapshot Manager.

Copying and Clearing Banks

The Mixer Snapshot Manager allows 4 independent banks of snapshots with ability to copy between banks and clear.

Rendering

The snapshot manager window relies on real time playback for auto recall. For faster-than-realtime rendering, this will lead to unpredictable results. Therefore, at render time, it is advisable to convert to real automation data. To do so, press Convert to Automation and optionally set which folder to use for gap detection (the conversion will also respect the switching mid-gap checkbox). Mixer, aux and submix tracks with snapshot data will appear in the arrange window along with any active automation envelopes. If items connected to mixer snapshots are moved on the timeline as part of editing, click on the convert button again to get instantly updated automation data. To clear the snapshot automation and return to auto recall via the window while editing and mixing, press Clear All Automation. Automation items that you created by hand on mixer, aux and submix tracks are protected: converting and clearing only replace the automation that the snapshots created.

Volume Automation

  1. Ensure that a "Destination" or "Source" track is selected.
  2. Make a time selection over the passage you want to change and press I. A time selection is required: changes that run from the cursor to the end of the piece are made with the Mixer Snapshot Manager instead.
  3. Set the volume level and optional ramp in/out lengths and click Apply Automation. The ramps lie outside the time selection: ramp in is the time before the selection and ramp out the time after it.

While you dial in the level you hear it immediately on playback; ramps cannot be previewed in this way. Check Keep window open after applying to make several adjustments in a row.

The first time you create an automation item, ReaClassical engages automation mode: items on the source folders are locked and ripple editing is set to all tracks, so a ripple edit on the destination folder carries the automation along with it. In horizontal workflow nothing is locked; only ripple editing changes. You can switch automation mode on and off yourself with Shift+I, from the ReaClassical menu or with the A button on the main toolbar (it replaces the marquee selection button). The button lights up and animates while automation mode is on.

More Advanced Automation

Turn on advanced mode to gain access to all envelopes associated with the track including FX parameters. If you also need to automate various aspects of the mixer tracks or special tracks, first make them visible in the track control panel by checking the box on the desired track row in Mission Control. Use I as before.

Editing Automation Items

Select an automation item and press Ctrl+I (or right-click on it) to edit its middle value and optional ramp in and out values. You can adjust the positioning by left-click dragging on the item itself. Adjust the middle value length by alt/opt-click dragging on automation item edges. Alt+D and Alt+E show and hide automation lanes, Shift+← and Shift+→ move between automation items and Ctrl+Shift+↑ and Ctrl+Shift+↓ move between envelope lanes.

Screen reader users (Clara)

Insert Automation (I) and Edit Automation (Ctrl+I) open keyboard-driven windows, the Automation Navigator and Accessible Edit Automation, in which you move between tracks, envelopes and values, and hear the level you are choosing while you dial it in.

General Mixing Workflow Suggestions

  • Set piece-by-piece "scenes" using the Mixer Snapshots Manager adjusting mixer tracks, aux and submix controls and any FX parameters.
  • Make temporary adjustments (for example, volume of spot microphones etc) via the automation function I on tracks with items.
  • For spot microphones that should be mostly muted: 1. Use a time selection + I to reduce to lowest value (-150dB/-inf) for the whole piece or use edit cursor + I at the beginning of the timeline to affect the whole project. 2. Use further time selections + I to set required values and any ramping in and out.

Tip

Remember that the mixer tracks (the ones starting "M:") are fed by the destination and source folders you see in the arrange window. In other words, any automation you add to destination or source tracks will be filtered through the mixer track state. As an example, if your violin spot microphone channel is set at -5dB via automation but the violin spot mixer track fader is at -40dB, the actual output will be -45dB.

Mixing for Dolby Atmos Using Fiedler Plugins

If you have the Fiedler Beam plugin on your system, use the Mission Control Enable Atmos that appears to add RCFader plugins and Fiedler Beam plugins to every Mixer track as necessary. This will also pass the current mixer fader values to the RCFader plugin. Subsequent presses of the button will check presence of RCFader and Fiedler plugins, and relative position between them, and synchronize fader values. Use Disable Atmos to deactivate both RCFader and Fiedler Beam plugins on every mixer track.

Mixing with Outboard Gear

Use the Mission Control HW Outputs to set direct connections to hardware either automatically or manually. If you do not need connections to RCMASTER, disable using the dedicated button in the main Mission Control window. Ctrl+Alt+Shift+T toggles the mute on RCMASTER's own hardware output sends (it mutes all of them if any is unmuted, and unmutes only when all are muted), and Alt+K is Panic Mute, which silences everything that can reach your hardware outputs.
