  • ↑ Up
  • Next →

Mastering

Mastering in ReaClassical is game-changing. Many features described here are not available in any other classical DAW. I hope that the ReaClassical way saves you much time and helps you look forward to the mastering phase of the project. While automatic DDP generation, automatic room tone function, and professional album reports are the main features here, you will probably find the revolutionary mixer snapshot manager is an extremely efficient way to add auto-recall mixer scenes across your production as well enjoying the ability to quickly reorder album tracks via a simple keyboard shortcuts.

Tip

ReaClassical treats the album as the items on the first track of the first folder, up to the first gap of more than 60 seconds between the end of one item and the start of the next. Everything after that gap is left out of the CD track markers, the album length and the album report. A gap of 60 seconds or less keeps the later material in the album. If working in horizontal workflow, ensure that there is more than 60 seconds of empty timeline between the end of the proposed album and any other source material. Instead, you can also choose to convert to a vertical workflow via Mission Control C, where source material lives in other folders. Show Statistics F1 reports how many items, and how much material, lie outside the album.

Basic Mastering Workflow

  1. The album is built on the first (destination) folder, so make sure your finished edit is there
  2. Remove all names from items on the parent track aside from those you want to be track starts. You can clear all items on the folder track via Ctrl+T
  3. Enter track start names via the Notes window N
  4. Press Y to open the metadata editor
  5. Once happy, use the Render buttons along the bottom of the metadata editor (see Rendering).

Note

In order to make the process as streamlined as possible for the user before the metadata editor window opens, on first run generic albumwide metadata (the name starts with "@") is added to an unnamed item on the parent folder. If that is not possible, a transparent split is made on the final item of the album.

Metadata Editor in Detail

The metadata window allows you to enter all track and album metadata in a single place.

  • Album metadata: title, performer, songwriter, composer, arranger, genre, identification, language, catalog (EAN/UPC) and message
  • Track metadata: title, performer, songwriter, composer, arranger, message and ISRC for each CD track

ISRC values are filled in automatically from the first track's entry, and the album-wide performer, songwriter, composer and arranger values are filled in from one or more entries in the track table. Check Manual ISRC entry or Manual Contributors Entry to override either. Right-click a field to copy its value to all tracks, to all later tracks, or from the album. Invalid ISRC and catalog entries are refused.

Screen reader users (Clara)

Y opens the accessible DDP Metadata Editor. ↑ and ↓ move between the tracks, Render Settings, Render, Album and CD Settings, and ← and → choose which metadata type (title, performer, songwriter, composer, arranger, message, ISRC) is read out for the current row. Enter edits the current cell and stops, so pressing ↓ and Enter repeatedly fills in one field down every track. Ctrl+A applies the current value to every track, Ctrl+R to this and the later tracks, Ctrl+P copies the previous track's value and Ctrl+U copies the album's. Read-only cells, such as the automatic album contributors or the automatic ISRC on tracks after the first, announce why they cannot be edited. CD Settings covers digital release, manual ISRC, pre/post roll and marker offsets.

Tip

Check the "!" box for CD tracks that you would like to have a visual countdown (length set in F5 prefs). This feature is not available in all CD players.

Recalculate

After moving CD start (named) items on the timeline, press Recalculate to refresh marker positions.

Digital Release Only

For those wanting to export individual media files only, check the "Digital Release Only" checkbox to ignore the CD offset value set in F5 preferences as well as disable the automatic snapping of markers and regions to CD frames. Then render with the WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320 buttons at the bottom of the editor.

Note

When this mode is enabled, you can still set manual marker offsets using the buttons in the metadata editor.

Repositioning and Re-arranging Album Tracks

There are two functions which help with reordering or repositioning tracks. First, and perhaps most useful for producing a classical album, is if you decide that you need to reorder one or more tracks. Select the named item you want to move either in the arrange window or metadata editor (by clicking on the track number) and press Move Album Track Up or Move Album Track Down (Ctrl+← and Ctrl+→ in the arrange window) to switch with the track immediately above or below it in the list. Note that gaps are preserved too. The other situation is when you want to start with uniform gaps between a series of short separate pieces. Use Reposition Album Tracks (Ctrl+Y) and enter a value in seconds. Your pieces are then automatically spaced and items crossfaded are left intact.

Marker Offsets

There may be instances when an audience member coughs right before a downbeat or a violinist hits strings before the first note of an otherwise excellent performance. The Add Marker Offset function allows you to adjust the start accordingly (assuming you have some nice recorded or generated roomtone on the dedicated roomtone track). To use, manually drag one or more CD markers to where you want them and then click Add Marker Offsets. It adds the correct offset(s) to the item name(s) automatically and refreshes the album metadata editor. Now, adjustments to an item position followed by a press of Y, maintains the relative CD marker offset to the item start. To remove all marker offsets, click Remove All Marker Offsets.

Multi-Disc Albums

Each disc is mastered as its own project, because the album is always built on a project's first folder. Make a project (or a project tab) per disc and run through the workflow above in each one. To compile material from several projects, see Multi-Project Tab S-D Editing.

Other Mastering Tips

CUE File and Reports

The Exports folder in your project folder collects the album listings: album_report.html and album_report.txt, and a complete technical metadata.txt file (useful for sending to a duplication/replication factory). A CUE file and a CD-Text (.cdt) file are written to Exports/Audio+CUE, next to the audio file made by the Cue Audio render button, so the CUE file's reference to the audio always resolves.

BIN+CUE set

Create a BIN/CUE pair (either select regions define tracks and render the whole project or select use only # markers and render by time selection if you don't want the first pre-gap as actual silence at the start of track 1).

Peak and Overs Check

Press Shift+P to scan every unmuted track that contains items. The window reports the highest peak level and its position, with a Go to Peak button, and lists every point at or above an over threshold (dB) that you set, each with a Go to button. The scan accounts for item and take volume (including a drawn volume envelope, if SWS is installed) and the faders along the routing chain up to RCMASTER, so it reflects the level arriving at the mix bus. Press Re-scan after making changes.

Screen reader users (Clara)

Shift+P opens an accessible Peak and Overs Check. On opening and on every rescan it announces the peak position and the number of overs and moves the edit cursor to the peak. You can then browse the overs one at a time, hear each over's level, position and track, and audition the peak.

CD Player

Press Ctrl+Alt+Shift+Y to play the album back like a physical CD player. The disc is always the first (destination) folder, and only it is heard. The player is a small window that needs keyboard focus, with buttons that mirror its keys for mouse users. When you switch it off with Escape, the cursor returns to where it was before you opened the player.

Key Action
P Play, pause or resume
S Stop, returning to the start of the disc
→ / ← Next track / previous track (restarts the current track if you are more than 3 seconds into it)
↑ / ↓ Fast forward / rewind
D Enter a track number (more than one digit allowed)
1 to 9 Jump straight to that track
T Cycle the time display: track elapsed, track remaining, album elapsed, album remaining
R Cycle repeat mode: off, track, album
B Toggle Transition Review
W Set the pre-roll and post-roll for Transition Review
H List these keys
Escape Power off

Transition Review plays only the joins: the start of the album, every transition between tracks, and the end of the album, each with a pre-roll before and post-roll after (10 seconds and 3 seconds by default). It is the quickest way to hear every splice and gap in a finished album without playing it through. The pregap before track 1 is not included. It reports "Nothing left to review" when it has played the last boundary.

Screen reader users (Clara)

The CD Player works fully from the keyboard and is announced: it says "Reading disc...", the track and time as you move, "Paused" and "Resumed", "No track N" if you ask for a track that does not exist, "Last track" at the end, the review pre- and post-roll values, and "CD Player off" when you close it.

Loudness

In terms of loudness, I personally aim for about -18 LUFS Integrated for my classical albums though it can be as high as -16 LUFS and as low as -20 LUFS. The new loudness JSFX meter in REAPER and my own ReaVision Metering Suite along with the normalization of loudness and true-peak limiting in the render dialog are priceless. It's another reason I couldn't go back to the other classical DAWs at this point.

Further information on DDP

For more information about DDP metadata see here (also available via the Render dialog via Format > DDP and clicking on Help).

Rendering

Rendering from the DDP Metadata Editor

Rendering is done with the Render buttons along the bottom of the DDP Metadata Editor window, which you open with Y (Create CD Markers). Each button applies its own settings and renders straight away, without showing REAPER's render dialog. The first (destination) folder is the one rendered, and the files go into an Exports subfolder of the project folder.

Button What it renders Where it goes
DDP A DDP image (44.1 kHz, 16-bit, triangular dither, as the Red Book standard requires) Exports/DDP/IMAGE.DAT with its companion files
Cue Audio The whole album as one audio file to pair with a CUE file Exports/Audio+CUE/
WAV One WAV file per CD track Exports/<format>_<samplerate>_<bitdepth>/
FLAC One FLAC file per CD track Exports/<format>_<samplerate>_<bitdepth>/
Opus 160 One 160 kbps Opus file per CD track (48 kHz) Exports/<format>_160/
MP3 320 One 320 kbps MP3 file per CD track Exports/<format>_320/
M: Stems One WAV per M: mixer track for each CD track, rendered through the master Exports/Stems_<format>_<samplerate>_<bitdepth>/
Custom Opens REAPER's render dialog, pre-filled with your choices to the left wherever you set

Files for individual CD tracks are named by CD track number and track name. In these per-track files, album and track metadata (titles, performers, ISRC and so on) is embedded where the format supports it, and if the project's media folder contains cover.jpg or cover.png (or folder.jpg or folder.png) it is embedded as cover art in MP3, FLAC and Opus files.

Three dropdowns next to the buttons set the sample rate, bit depth and dither for Cue Audio, WAV, FLAC, M: Stems and Custom. DDP always uses the Red Book settings. Opus renders at 48 kHz, and MP3 uses 32, 44.1 or 48 kHz, whichever the chosen sample rate divides into cleanly. The Tracks box limits WAV, FLAC, Opus, MP3 and M: Stems to particular CD tracks, for example 1-3,5; leave it blank to render every track. DDP, Cue Audio and Custom always render the full album.

Before rendering, ReaClassical checks your metadata and warns about text that DDP and CD-Text cannot hold (characters outside Latin-1, embedded line breaks), duplicated ISRC codes and tracks without a title.

Screen reader users (Clara)

The accessible DDP Metadata Editor has a Render Settings row (sample rate, bit depth and dither) and a Render row where you choose the format and then, if it applies, a track range such as 1-3,5. Progress and warnings are announced through Clara.

To export every recorded take for the musicians or a producer, see Distributing Takes On Location.

REAPER's Render Dialog

You can still open REAPER's own render dialog with R. In it, click on the presets button then All Settings. ReaClassical adds presets for DDP, BIN+CUE, Audio for CUE export, Export for External Resampling, and FLAC, WAV, MP3 and Opus at common sample rates and bit depths. After selecting a preset, you should feel free to change any render settings and perhaps save as a new preset for future use.

Samplerate

Now that r8brain free has been introduced as the best quality resampler available in REAPER (I highly recommend double-checking that it is selected when resampling at render time) I feel I can do everything, including DDP creation, without leaving my favorite DAW. However, generating a CUE file via the Create CD Markers function is still useful for all sorts of things and I often create FLAC + CUE for album playback in my media player or WAV + CUE to easily burn a CD at home. The Cue Audio button renders the whole album as a single file next to its CUE file for exactly this.

Dither

The Render row offers sample rates of 44.1, 48, 88.2, 96, 176.4 and 192 kHz, bit depths of 16, 24 and 32-bit float, and dither of Triangular, HP filtered, Noise shaping or Off. Dither and noise shaping are applied by the render, so choose Off if you prefer to use RCDither or another 3rd-party dither as the last plugin on the master chain. In that case be sure to keep the master fader at unity.

Loudness & Limiting

REAPER has a fantastic rendering feature which allows the user to set a desired loudness and peak / true peak setting. For quick exports that need to meet certain targets (i.e. streaming) this makes things extremely efficient and is very transparent when not set to extreme values.

Dry-run Rendering

Another REAPER feature that is outstanding is the dry-run render function which allows for very quick offline loudness and peak checks and much faster than using REAPER's included realtime loudness meter. It is therefore extremely easy to set up compressors, limiters etc in the project and make small adjustments based on the dry-run values and maintain complete control over the process.

Other Rendering Tips

Not necessarily obvious to new REAPER users are the special =START and =END markers (make your markers in the usual way and label them accordingly) that constrain the length of the project. Rather than rely on extended silence at the end of items or time selections, the =END marker is a great way to ensure you have the exact amount of lead-out you want at the end of the disc. You will hopefully notice I have included various shortcuts for manually creating regions (single or multiple) from items and time selection (great for quickly generating demo snippets). Also worth noting is that you can still do some (or all!) of your source-destination editing with your track markers in place as the S/D markers have IDs far higher than any classical CD would have and are automatically deleted after a successful edit. As long as you have your ripple-per-track mode engaged, all your existing marker placements and carefully crafted edits will remain intact. But, again, don't manually create CD markers at this point as I include a very powerful tool to make light work of that side of mastering.

Collaborating with Video Editors

When working on projects that combine audio and video, the audio engineer must ensure that high-resolution audio edits remain synchronized with the final assembled video. Several approaches exist:

No audio edits required – The simplest case. The video editor is free to select camera angles without concerns about audio sync.

Post-edited audio with playback – The promotional video is recorded after the audio has been edited, with musicians miming or playing along to playback via loudspeaker. The video editor has complete freedom to cut between angles without sync issues. This method isn't always feasible.

Minor edits in live-recorded video – When video and audio are recorded simultaneously and only minor edits are needed, the video editor can use a zoomed-out shot of the concert hall, a musician's face, or another visual to mask a slight time-stretch while preserving timecode accuracy.

Multiple synchronized takes – The most complex scenario. Both video and audio are recorded in multiple takes and synchronized via a timeclock. This is the focus of the following discussion.

ReaClassical provides tools to generate an edit list for video editors. Rather than a file for direct import, this list serves as a manual reference. For all recordings, but especially those synchronized to a timeclock, REAPER/ReaClassical retains the timeline start position from the recording. This ensures that absolute in/out source positions can be retrieved even after extensive audio edits. To create an edit list:

  1. Perform source-destination edits as usual.
  2. Set the desired project framerate in the video tab of Project Settings via P.
  3. Export the edit list from the ReaClassical menu under Utilities, using the shortcut for the version you need:
    1. Build Edit List (using BWF Start Offset) (Alt+Shift+B) for timeclock-synced projects. It asks for an optional offset in frames, applied to every time in the list.
    2. Build Edit List (using source file timing) (Ctrl+Shift+B) to reference positions inside the source audio files. In this case, the audio engineer should provide a single channel of audio to help the video editor locate edit points, and the list also includes the source files used.

The edit list opens in your web browser as an HTML table with a Done column for tracking progress. When an offset is used, the page states it in red at the top, so the video editor knows the times have been shifted.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need my own REAPER license?

ReaClassical installs its own portable copy of REAPER, so there is nothing to download from Cockos first. REAPER itself is separately licensed software: after its evaluation period you should buy a REAPER license from Cockos.

Can I install ReaClassical into my existing REAPER?

No. The installer creates a separate, self-contained ReaClassical folder with REAPER and everything pre-configured (resource files, theme, keymap and plugins), and installing into an existing setup, including by importing the ReaPack repository on its own, is not supported. See Install.

What if I only want the source-destination editing functions?

You do not need ReaClassical for that. ReaEdit is a free, separate package that adds source-destination editing to regular REAPER, with its own manual at reaclassical.com/reaedit. If you use ReaClassical you already have all of these functions, and many more, so you do not need ReaEdit and should not install it.

Is ReaClassical free?

Yes. ReaClassical and ReaEdit are free and open source, released under the GNU General Public License version 3. There is no license key, no account and no activation. See Licensing.

How many computers can I use?

As many as you like. There are no seats or machine limits.

Does ReaClassical work offline?

The installer needs an internet connection. After that ReaClassical works entirely offline: nothing checks a license or contacts a server while you work. You only need the internet again when you ask for a download: Update ReaClassical, Update REAPER, the Terminal clara command, or an update through ReaPack. REAPER's own projects, of course, are ordinary local files.

Can I carry ReaClassical on a USB drive between computers?

Yes. A ReaClassical folder is portable, so you can copy it to a USB drive and run it on any computer of the same operating system.

Can my school, university or studio use it on many computers?

Yes, on as many computers as you like.

What information does ReaClassical send?

None about you or your work. It never uploads your audio or projects. The installer, Update ReaClassical, Update REAPER, the Terminal clara command and ReaPack download files when you ask them to, which is the only network activity. See the Privacy Policy.

Which operating systems are supported?

Windows (x64, x86 and ARM64), macOS (Apple silicon, 64-bit Intel and 32-bit Intel) and Linux (x86_64, i686, aarch64 and armv7l, including Raspberry Pi). See Compatibility.

Can I use my existing REAPER projects?

Yes. Open the project and use Project Management > Convert REAPER project in the ReaClassical menu. It converts the project in a new tab, flattens folders, deletes empty tracks and moves effects to the mixer tracks, leaving you to recreate any custom routing in Mission Control. See Converting a Standard REAPER Project.

Can I open my ReaClassical projects in regular REAPER?

Yes. A ReaClassical project is an ordinary REAPER project: a standard .RPP file with your normal audio files, so it opens, plays and renders in any current vanilla REAPER, on any machine, with or without ReaClassical. Your recordings, edits, crossfades, markers and mix are all still there. What regular REAPER does not have is the specialist ReaClassical tooling that makes the work efficient: the recording workflow, source-destination and crossfade editing, Mission Control, mixer snapshots, the mastering tools, the DDP metadata editor and so on. Those exist only in ReaClassical. If the project uses ReaClassical's own plugins (the RCPlugs collection), install them in the other REAPER too, or regular REAPER will show those plugins as missing.

Should I choose a horizontal or vertical workflow?

Neither is better; each has its advantages. In a horizontal workflow, recorded or imported takes are arranged left to right in a single folder. A vertical workflow helps organize like material in a recording session: takes of the same musical material are recorded vertically aligned, one folder per take. Functions such as finding a take by number work the same way in both, so choose whichever matches how you like to see your session. You can convert between them later in Mission Control. See Project Setup.

Why can't I rename, add or delete tracks the normal REAPER way?

ReaClassical keeps a set of linked tracks in step with each other (the folders, the M: mixer tracks, aux and submix busses and the routing between them). Doing track management outside Mission Control breaks that link. If you do it by accident, open Mission Control (C) and it will recreate what is missing.

How do I start a recording?

Select the parent track of a folder and press F9. This opens the Record Panel and arms the folder. See Recording.

Where do my recordings go?

Into a media subfolder of the project folder by default. You can change the primary and secondary recording paths in REAPER's Project Settings (P), on the Media tab.

How do I give the musicians the takes while I'm still on location?

Press Ctrl+Shift+D (Distribute Takes, called Quick Export Recorded Takes in the ReaClassical menu). It exports every recorded take as WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320 into the project's Exports/Distribute_Takes folder, using your mixer settings. See Distributing Takes On Location.

How do I import audio recorded in another DAW?

Name the files with a track name and a take number at the end, such as cello_012.wav, put them in the project's media folder and run Smart Import (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+I). Multi-channel files from a portable recorder are handled on the Polywav tab. See Importing.

How do I make a source-destination edit?

Set destination IN and OUT markers with 1 and 2, source IN and OUT markers with 3 and 4, and press 5. Press F on the right-hand item of the crossfade to fine-tune it. See Editing.

How do I undo or repair an edit?

Ctrl+Z undoes the last action. To restore the material underneath an earlier S-D edit, select it and press Ctrl+H to heal it. If items that should be grouped have become misaligned across the tracks of a folder, for example because ripple-per-track was switched off by accident while dragging items, select any one of them and run Fix Crossfade Sequence Edits (Shift+X).

Why do my mixer scenes not sound right in a render?

Mixer snapshots are recalled in real time during playback, which does not work for a faster-than-realtime render. Before rendering, press Convert to Automation in the Mixer Snapshot Manager. See Mixing.

How do I make a DDP image?

Open the DDP Metadata Editor with Y, fill in your album and track metadata and click the DDP button along the bottom. The result is in the Exports/DDP folder of the project. See Mastering and Rendering.

How do I render each CD track as a separate file?

Use the WAV, FLAC, Opus 160 or MP3 320 buttons in the DDP Metadata Editor. Choose the sample rate, bit depth and dither first, and limit the tracks with the Tracks box if you only need some of them. See Rendering.

What loudness should I aim for?

That depends on where the music is going. The author aims for about -18 LUFS integrated for classical albums, and anywhere between -20 and -16 LUFS is reasonable. REAPER's render dialog can also normalize to a loudness target and apply true-peak limiting, and a dry run gives you quick loudness and peak values without a full render.

Can I use my own plugins?

Yes. Any plugin that works in REAPER works in ReaClassical, and Mission Control lets you add FX to the mixer tracks. ReaClassical also comes with a set of mastering-grade JSFX plugins. See Recommended Free Mastering-Grade Plugins.

Can blind and low-vision engineers use ReaClassical?

Yes. With the Clara accessibility bridge installed, ReaClassical announces what it is doing and provides keyboard-driven windows and modes for every stage of a production. See the Accessibility section.

How do I update ReaClassical, and how do I reset it?

Press Shift+U (Update ReaClassical) to receive the latest version of your major release. A new major version needs a fresh install. To return to the settings from first install, use ReaClassical Factory Reset (Ctrl+Alt+Shift+F). See Update.

Is there a PDF manual, and where do I get help?

There is no PDF. The manual is online at https://reaclassical.com/manual and a single-page copy is installed with ReaClassical (press H). For support, see Community and Support.

Keyboard Shortcuts

When providing keyboard shortcuts, this manual assumes Windows or Linux as the operating system when modifier keys are used. MacOS users should use the typical standard substitutions. If in doubt, open up the actions menu via keyboard shortcut ? or explore the top "ReaClassical" menu to see the current assignments. For reference (from REAPER's own user guide), here is a table of equivalent modifier keys:

PC (Windows or Linux) Key Mac (MacOS) Key Equivalent
Shift Shift
Control (Ctrl) Command (Cmd)
Alt Option
Windows Control

The best way of becoming familiar with ReaClassical keyboard shortcuts is to hover over buttons in Mission Control C and the S-D editing toolbar F6, but most of all, explore the top "ReaClassical" menu inbetween "Options" and "Extensions".

Other Keys

Besides ReaClassical's own functions, the ReaClassical keymap assigns keys to a handful of REAPER and SWS actions:

Keys Action
O / P / R REAPER Preferences / Project Settings / Render dialog
Ctrl+F9 Pause
Ctrl+- / Ctrl+= Rewind / fast forward a little
Ctrl+_ / Ctrl++ Move the cursor one pixel left / right
Ctrl+↑ / Ctrl+↓ Increase / decrease the peaks display zoom
Ctrl+P Clear all peak indicators
Alt+M Insert and/or edit a marker at the current position
: / ; Insert a region from the time selection / from the selected items (named by the active take)
/ Set the time selection to the selected items
0 Deselect all items
L Region and marker manager
Ctrl+E View envelopes for the current or last touched track
Ctrl+Shift+N Move the edit cursor to the next envelope point and select it
Alt+Shift+E or Ctrl+Shift+E Add or edit the envelope point value at the cursor
Tab Move the cursor to the item's peak sample (SWS)
Alt+Shift+H Trim or untrim the item's left edge to the edit cursor (SWS/Xenakios)
NumPad + Switch to the next project tab
Shift+B Batch file converter

The Shortcuts Guide

A complete, searchable list of every ReaClassical shortcut is available as a web page, generated from the keymap that ships with ReaClassical so it is always accurate. Open it offline from the ReaClassical menu with Shortcuts Guide, or online at https://reaclassical.com/rcshortcuts.html. Type in the search box to filter by action name, mode or key.

The Mode column matters. "Normal" shortcuts work everywhere. The other values are keyboard modes with their own keys: Crossfade Mode, Item Edit Mode, Mixer Mode and Recording mode (see Keyboard Modes), and the two-lane crossfade editor's own shortcuts. The same key can mean something different in each mode.

Screen reader users (Clara)

Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H (Menu Help) walks through the ReaClassical menu with a screen reader, announcing the shortcut for each item, so you can explore the available functions without leaving REAPER.

Recommended Free Mastering-Grade Plugins

First stop: Reaplugs , with particular mention of ReaLimit which I consider one of the best free transparent limiter available. You could easily mix and master a whole album using only these fine plugins. Others include:

Analysis

ReaVision (ReaClassical metering suite). Your one-stop shop for loudness and true peak values as well as adjustable K-meter, goniometer (with adjustable visual boost), phase correlation meter, bitmeter, spectrum analyzer and spectrograph.

EQ

RCChannelEQ (ReaClassical Channel EQ, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in ReaPack via my repository). Uses DSP from airwindows Baxandall and Stillwell's RBJ Highpass/Lowpass Filters for broad-strokes EQing.

RCMasteringEQ (ReaClassical Mastering EQ, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in ReaPack via my repository). Uses DSP from airwindows Hull2 with added Range drop-down (Classical or Full) for transparent, musical, broad-strokes EQing.

ReEQ https://forum.cockos.com/showthread.php?t=213501. An amazing Fabfilter Pro-Q clone for detailed EQ work. Also comes with ReSpectrum which is an excellent analyzer. Both are included with the ReaClassical install.

Compression

RCCompressor (ReaClassical compressor, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Uses DSP from Express Bus Compressor by Stillwell. Default settings and ranges tuned to classical music with auto release. Use as an insert.

RCParallelK (ReaClassical parallel Katz compressor, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Also uses DSP from Express Bus Compressor by Stillwell to recreate the Bob Katz transparent parallel compression settings. There's only a make-up gain slider as everything else is baked in (-50dB threshold, 2.5:1 ratio, 1ms attack, peak detection mode). Use on a dedicated compressor bus and adjust the gain slider to taste (with the compressor signal somewhere between -15dB and -5dB lower than dry signal according to Katz).

Limiter

RCLimiter (ReaClassical limiter, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Uses DSP from Smooth Limiter by Geraint Luff to which I added 4x oversampling code. Defaults are tuned to classical music with true-peak and look-ahead functionality. Adjust the release to taste.

Reverb

Algorithmic: For a free option try my RCReverb (ReaClassical reverb, port of zita-rev1, included in the ReaClassical portable install as part of RCPlugs collection). For paid options, ValhallaDSP Room and Vintage Verb, Fabfilter Pro-R, Voxengo Sobor, Acon Digital Verberate 2 and Sonible smart:reverb are all excellent non-iLok options for classical music and work seamlessly via yabridge on Linux. Note that the Liquidsonics offerings no longer require a physical iLok so can also be used on Linux via yabridge and iLok Cloud activation if you are feeling brave.

Convolution: Convology XT (also runs perfectly at time of writing via yabridge on Linux) coupled with the Samplicity Bricasti M7 impulses. There are other free convolution plugins to use but, whatever the plugin choice, the Bricasti impulses in true stereo are fantastic and sound almost identical to the presets of the well-regarded Liquidsonics Seventh Heaven Professional.

Final Mastering Magic

Sonnox Inflator -style wave-shaping: Try RCInflator Ultimate (a clone of the Sonnox product) or MagicFairyDust on the final stereo bus. Both effects are included in the ReaClassical portable install.

Console vibe: Use the RCConsoleChannel , RCConsoleBus , and RCConsoleFinalizer at the end of regular tracks, busses and final 2-bus respectively. Note that RCConsoleChannel does not have any controls.

Restoration

Bertom Denoiser Classic https://www.bertomaudio.com/. Denoiser Pro ($25) allows for individual per-band thresholds and includes an adaptive mode.

RCDeEss Standard (ReaClassical de-esser, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Uses DSP from airwindows DeEss.

RCDeEss Advanced (ReaClassical advanced de-esser, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Uses DSP from airwindows DeBess.

Utilities

RCGain (ReaClassical gain plugin, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Uses DSP from airwindows PurestGain. Useful before or after plugins in lieu of a native channel trim knob.

JS Loudness Meter Peak/RMS/LUFS (Cockos) (included with REAPER).

RCTime &PhaseTool (ReaClassical timing and phase tool, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Add to a spot microphone channel. Achieves something similar to Merging's PanNoir to correctly align spot microphone channels with the main pair based on a fundamental Euclidean geometric relation to create a more impactful stereo image.

RCMidSide (ReaClassical mid-side encoder-decoder, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Use the default decoder mode if wanting to convert recorded mid-side to regular left-right stereo.

RCDither (ReaClassical dither plugin, included in the ReaClassical portable install and available in my repository). Uses DSP from airwindows Not-Just-Another-Dither (Monitoring version) here called Avant-garde. This just might be the world's finest dither. There's a drop-down to select between 16-bit and 24-bit.

For descriptions of the other 100+ jsfx airwindows ports (covering dithers, compressors, console emulations, saturation/distortion, delays, bass-specific, brightness, hard and soft clippers, reverbs, tape/vinyl emulations, exciters, stereo wideners, monitoring utilities and more, please see the dedicated REAPER forums thread and import the airwindows JSFX ports repository into ReaPack.

Room Tone Generation

In File > Project Templates you will find a room tone generation template. The method is derived from here. To create endless room tone based on the venue you recorded:

  1. Click Browse in ReaVerb and select your few seconds of recorded reverb.
  2. Enable the FX on the first mixer track
  3. Adjust the length of the included region to the length of your live album
  4. Render using Bounds > All project regions

Save the rendered file as roomtone.wav in your ReaClassical project's media folder. When you add a Room Tone track via Mission Control, ReaClassical imports roomtone.wav onto it automatically (it is never overwritten if the track already has an item). Each time you run Create CD Markers via Y, the room tone item is trimmed to end at the =END marker, or at the end of the last item on the first folder if that marker does not exist yet, and automation-based fades are added to coincide with opposite fade types on the first track, creating perfect crossfades into room tone and back without any fuss. If the room tone audio is shorter than the album, you are warned how many seconds short it is.

System Tweaks

Windows

For a modern Windows 10/11 setup, required tweaks are minimal. Ensure that you are using 'High Performance' or ideally 'Ultimate Performance'. which, if not available, can be activated by opening a command prompt and pasting:

powercfg -duplicatescheme e9a42b02-d5df-448d-aa00-03f14749eb61

You can then select it from the usual power plan dialog. For best device performance, remember to use the ASIO drivers that were included with your audio interface. Consider disabling your network card during mission-critical recording. For further tips see Microsoft's Unofficial Windows 10 and 11 Audio Workstation build and tweak guide. Of particular interest is Part 3 which discusses what not to do (including not setting your processor scheduling to 'background services').

MacOS

Performance should be excellent out of the box. Remember to disable energy saving (System Settings > Energy on recent macOS, or System Preferences > Energy Saver on older versions) so that sessions are not interrupted. Consider disabling your network card during mission-critical recording. If you are experiencing any audio issues while in your DAW, for tips see Focusrite's optimization page.

GNU/Linux

Linux users should visit my Arch Pro Audio Guide. Performance out of the box on Linux is getting better with every kernel release and is on par or better than Windows. As a starting point, ensure that your username is set up for realtime privileges (step 3), that the threadirqs kernel parameter is set (step 4) and that you are running the performance CPU governor (step 5). Check that your kernel is fully preemptible too (see the guide's introduction). To make things even easier, consider using a dedicated audio/video distro like AVLinux or Ubuntu Studio where everything is already set up for you.

Cross-platform

The good news is that REAPER and ReaClassical run on many different architectures and operating systems. You should always be able to open up a project on another machine even if it is running a different OS. Plus, ReaClassical includes various mastering-grade plugins in JSFX format that run on all architectures.
